-in fact all the nations now fighting for freedom with the exception of the Union of Soviet Socialist Republics. They have been invited, but so far I have no news of their acceptance or otherwise of the invitation. The conference meets under the high sponsorship of Roosevelt, Churchill and of our own Prime Minister. It meets here because- and I say it advisedly and without either false modesty or vain boasting-Canada, of all the nations now engaged in fighting this war, has made the greatest progress in training men to conquer the air and to wrest the supremacy of the air from the enemy so as to pave the way to victory.
These delegates come here to observe what has been done, to note the methods followed, to consult with us as to the means to be taken, to endeavour to coordinate our efforts and those of our commonwealth partners into a world-wide united nations programme. This, as the newspaper has said, is indeed a tribute to Canada. And when I say "Canada" I mean, all Canada; for Canada has been the administrator of the greatest undertaking ever instituted within its territory. It has been successfully carried out, may I say in, all frankness and all sincerity, not by the Department of National Defence for Air, not by the government, not even by the Royal Canadian Air Force, but by the people of the whole dominion, every section of which has made its contribution. From the very inception this plan has been non-political and nonsectional, and all parties in this house and the entire press have joined in making it a success. It is unique, I will say, as an instance of a great undertaking which hitherto has escaped political or sectional criticism.
At the very moment when the united nations are meeting here to discuss this great project of our united Canadian nation, we are in the midst of an internal crisis the gravity and seriousness of which I would and should be the last to minimize. When one
has campaigned and marched and bivouacked and fought for twenty-five years with friends, it is a sad wrench indeed to be separated from them, even temporarily. Our own country is apparently torn asunder, not on the question of the war itself but on the methods to be employed by Canada in waging war. There is, I am glad to say, no difference of opinion with respect to the air war, either as to the raising of men or money or the spheres of action. I wonder if, during the time the representatives of all our allies are here, it would be possible to call a truce to our internal dissensions and show by a united front, temporary if you will, our determination to join with them in the defeat of the common enemy.

We have listened to-day to a report of the progress of the air force under the Minister of National Defence for Air. At the close of his remarks he made an appeal for unity in this country. May I say to him as an old soldier, and speaking I believe for most of us in this chamber, that no matter where we march or where we bivouac we shall find that, under the Minister of National Defence for Air, we shall go forward in the great effort which he is making in furtherance of this project. To-day he has given us concrete evidence of what has been accomplished, beginning as it did in a very small way. To-day, as he has stated, we are on the eve of a conference of the united nations. Under his leadership this enterprise, so soundly based, the British commonwealth air training plan, is certain to develop rapidly and with increasing success.
I have only one or two remarks to add to what has already been said. I wish particularly to refer to the system of air cadet training, which has developed from one of the minister's own policies. Looking at it from the viewpoint of my own province and as I have observed it elsewhere, I feel that, once established by the department, it has been left rather in the position of an orphan. We have been loath to give these organizations the blessing of the department while we have been willing to say to them, "You go out and do it." If we are prepared to accept the air cadets in Canada, as I am sure we are from the minister's remarks and from what has been said; if we are prepared to have them established, then we should establish air cadets as part and parcel of the air scheme of the dominion. We should assist them and give them the support that is necessary and not put them on the basis of some service plan, as has been done. I believe that if the minister will look into the matter he will find that the air cadets proposal, supported by himself and promulgated

War Appropriation-Air Services
by his department, has not been given the support by the government that it should have received. If the air cadets are to be part and parcel of the air force, let us make them so. Do not let us have any half measures whereby we make them cadets for one purpose and not for another. The Minister of National Defence for Air will be the first to admit that they should be made part and parcel of the air force.
The other matter I have to urge is in connection with the air crew, to which the minister has referred. I have watched, as I have no doubt other members have watched, the graduation of air crews from various schools throughout the country. I am told that ninety schools have been established, and day after day we see men walking our streets, pilots, gunners, and observers and other members of the crews to whom the minister has referred. I want to make a plea as a man who served as an ordinary private soldier in the last war, and it is this, that these men who are worthy of wearing wings, whether they be pilots, observers, gunners or whatever they may be, should be commissioned in the air force and should not be put into the ranks as sergeant observers, sergeant pilots, or sergeant gunners, as the case may be. I urge that they be given equal rank and that they be not classed on the basis of 50 per cent of this particular class or that particular class. Those of us who have gone through schools will know that in one particular class there may be 90 per cent who may be worthy of a commission, whereas in some other class there may be only 40 per cent or 30 per cent. It is my opinion that so long as you leave it to the officers commanding the various schools there will be discrepancies that should not exist. If a man is capable of graduating from a school and worthy of his wings, whether he be pilot, observer or gunner, then he is worthy of being commissioned in his majesty's service. I urge upon the minister that this discrepancy be abolished, because I know it must have given him more than one headache. Take two buddies graduating from an air force school about to leave the country. They are on their last leave, arranging to meet at a certain port to go overseas, arranging to occupy the same quarters on the same transport. One receives word while he is at home that he has been commissioned, the other receives no such news and will go over as a sergeant pilot. You cannot expect absolute team-work under those conditions. I know the minister will agree with me that in this great service, the air force, the important thing is team-work, and you cannot get it unless you ensure that two men who are going forth in the same service shall 
be in the same rank if they are doing the same job. When they graduate from a particular school they should be on the same level. It is not fair or worthy that some commanding officer should be allowed to say to one, "You shall be a commissioned pilot", and to another "You shall be a sergeant pilot".	[DOT]
I urge that this question be given careful consideration at the forthcoming conference of the united nations-the United States, Canada, Great Britain and the other countries who will meet here. They will recognize the lead that Canada has given, and I hope that out of that conference there will emerge the principle of equality with regard to the men who graduate from our schools, whether they be pilots, gunners, observers, or whatever they may be. So long as they are worthy of going into the air and operating planes they should be put on an equality. We see men walking around the streets to-day and we know that this equality does not exist. This has been a source of trouble to the minister, I am sure; it has been one of the headaches from which he has suffered. I say to him that instead of cutting down 50 per cent, or 30 per cent or 20 per cent of the graduates of a class, every man who is worthy to wear the wings should be a commissioned officer in his majesty's services.

There are one or two matters I should like to bring to the attention of the minister, and I want to ask some questions in connection with the statement that he has just made. Before I do so, however, may I congratulate him on the complete and at the same time the concise manner in which he has given us the information which he has put before us this afternoon. The minister painted a glowing picture of the commonwealth air training plan, and I am sure that all hon. members will agree with him that Canada is indeed proud of the contribution it is making in this regard. Certainly to most of us it is our greatest contribution. In any event, it is certainly the most romantic, one of the most interesting, and one which we in Canada are eminently fitted to make. The tragedy of our reverses in the war up to the present time has been unfortuna.tely the result of lack of air strength or air superiority. Unquestionably if we had had that air superiority we would not have suffered the reverses we did in Crete, we would possibly be in command of the situation so far as the far east is concerned, and we would not be faced with the gigantic problem we have in connection with the shortage of rubber and matters of that kind, which I am sorry to say is crippling a part of our war effort.

War Appropriation-Air Services
In the course of his comments the minister made no reference, as he did last year, to the headaches that bothered him at that time. I presume that most of those difficulties have been solved.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: No, I was expecting hon. members to tell me. I have new ones.

Last year the minister
referred to certain headaches, as he called them, in the plan, and out of this discussion and the questions that will be asked here, I have no doubt that we shall ascertain how many of these headaches are still there and how many have disappeared. In connection with the commonwealth air training plan itself the minister indicated last year, and I believe he corroborated it in his statement this afternoon, that the new plan had been pretty well completed and we are now in the process referred to last year as being "levelled off". If I am wrong in that regard he will correct me. May I ask him whether or not the S344,000,000 which has been appropriated for the joint commonwealth air training plan is the figure which he estimates will be required annually for the carrying on of this plan, or is there in that figure a sum which has been set aside for the purpose of extending the plan? Has he completed the whole picture with respect to establishments across the country?

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: Yes.
I refer particularly to air training schools.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: No new aerodromes, if I can help it. That is a headache.

That was one of the first headaches I was going to refer to. My question is whether or not a part of that $344,000,000 is intended to be used for extension, whether the minister had in contemplation, as a result of the coming conference, any extension of the plan in Canada; whether he had in contemplation setting up any additional schools and aerodromes across the country. I know the minister, as he stated last year, has been greatly concerned over the pressure that has been brought to bear on him and on the department with respect to the establishment of such schools, and that sort of thing, and my thought was that if he did contemplate an extension as a result of this conference which begins next week; if he should decide to build more aerodromes and set up more service training schools and the like in Canada, he might very well state at the outset that matters of representations, and what we might call pressure, will receive
not the slightest regard as far as the selection of these places is concerned. I feel sure the minister has paid very little attention to that sort of thing in the past; but if he should expand the plan I believe that by announcing in the first place that pressure of this kind would have no effect, he might head off this deluge of delegations, representations by boards of trade, members of parliament and that sort of thing, and thereby save himself and probably the country a very great headache.
During the course of his remarks the minister made some statements in connection with recruits and the number of men now being turned out by the air force. Among other things I think he said there were now some 115,000 men in the R.C.A.F. When the minister makes a further statement during this discussion I should like him to indicate, on the same basis that he indicated last year, the proportion of the men in training in Canada who are Canadians and the proportion who come from Australia, New Zealand and Great Britain. At the same time he might indicate, if he will, in greater detail what is being done in connection with this reserve that was set up last year. At that time the minister referred to the fact that there was a six months' reserve on hand. Again this year he has referred to the fact that there is a six months' reserve on hand. What is being done with these men? As I recall it, last year they were being enlisted two or three months ahead of time and being put on guard duty, and that sort of thing. But conditions must have been altered to some extent by the calling up of men under the National Resources Mobilization Act and by the pressure that is being exerted in connection with recruiting for the army. What steps are being taken by the department to ensure that the reserve, which the minister called a "precious" reserve, is maintained, to be called upon as soon as the training facilities are available?
There are so many questions to be asked in connection with the minister's department that I intend to mention only one or two now, hoping later on in the debate to be able to put specific and categorical questions to the minister. In connection with repairs and equipment, the minister stated that at present he had enough planes to meet the requirements. From this statement I presume that the deficit from which he suffered last year, particularly the shortage of twin-engine machines, of which the minister said last year he had only 46 per cent of what was required, has been made up. At the same

War Appropriation-Air Services
time I should like the minister to give us some indication, if he would, of how far his department has advanced toward the objective of 6,000 planes for training purposes, which he said would be required by 1943. At the time the minister spoke last year he said they had 2,400 machines on hand. Now, after a year's progress, and with the passing of half the period mentioned by the minister, I should like to know how many planes he has on hand for training purposes, and whether he anticipates that he will obtain the required number of 6,000 by 1943.
There is another point that seems to me most important. Last year the minister said the matter of repairs, replacements, spare parts and so on, was giving him a great deal of concern. He did not mention that matter this afternoon. In view of the fact that the United States, from whom we obtained a great many of these spares, is now in the war, has its own training plan, and is producing aeroplanes for its own use, has the situation been alleviated or made more difficult than before? If it has become more difficult, what safeguards does the minister anticipate putting into effect in order to make sure that accidents in training, for example, do not occur, and that the men who are training in Canada have the very best of equipment and the very safest facilities, in order that they may complete that training?
With further reference to the matter of recruiting, the minister mentioned that he had obtained a considerable number of men who had been called up; I think he referred to them as R recruits. I presume he meant men who, after they had been called up, in some way had been brought into the air force. Was that as a result of the air force or the [DOT]army going to these men and inquiring whether or not they wanted to join the air force, or was it because after they were called up they indicated a desire to join the air force?

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: After they were called up.

In that connection the minister mentioned last year that he was very much in favour of what he called "combing the mane to sharpen the tooth," I think borrowing an expression used by Mr. Churchill-in other words obtaining recruits from the active army. Is there any question of canvassing the active army, to determine whether or not there are men in it who are particularly qualified to become pilots, gunners, and so on, and who would be of more value to Canada's war effort if they were trained as such? In that connection I can understand that the minister might come in conflict with the Minister of National Defence, who naturally would not want to lose any men from the army. But I 
suggest that there are in the air force a great many men who enlisted for general duty. The minister mentioned that some of those men were being reclassified, but there must be a great many of them who are not qualified to become pilots or air crew, but who at the same time are physically fit and who could go on active service. I suggest to the minister that he might consider taking up with his colleague the Minister of National Defence the possibility of working out some system under which these general duty men could be transferred to the army, and men taken from the army who could be trained to become air crew. After all, I take it that maintaining a sufficient number of recruits for air crew is the most important part of the whole plan, because if you have not the men the plan becomes completely useless. I should think the minister could replace a great many of these general duty men-and I understand this is being done to a certain extent-with medically unfit men, ex-service men perhaps, and particularly with the new branch which has been set up, the women's branch of the air force. As I understand it, that was the original purpose in setting up this women's division, and perhaps the minister would give us some idea of the extent to which these women are replacing men in the air force and permitting them to be transferred to more active theatres of war.
I should like to offer a suggestion to the minister with regard to a matter which has been brought up on several occasions during the discussion of this war appropriation bill, with particular reference to the army and navy. It has to do with the question of the pay and allowances of men in the air force, particularly with respect to the fact that a distinction is made between the air force and the army in the case of men who are missing. So far as the air force is concerned, the dependents' allowance is cut off at the end of the month during which the man is reported missing, whereas in the army the pay and allowances are continued for a longer period of time. The other day the Minister of National Defence told us that in the army, pay and allowances are continued until the man is either presumed dead or it is definitely established that he is dead.
So far as the air force is concerned my information, which I have reason to believe is accurate, is that if a man is reported as missing in- the middle of the month his pay is computed until the end of the month and sent to his wife. Thereafter however she is immediately put on straight pension, and her income is consequently immediately reduced to the 160 a month provided for the

War Appropriation-Air Services
wives of those up to and including the rank of flying officer. It seems to me that that is a discrimination which the minister should take in hand and remove. The wife of a man reported missing suffers a terrific shock, and she is at the same time faced with considerable financial difficulty, particularly if her income is immediately cut down. I have known it to be cut down by as much as $25 or $30 a month. I have known of children being born to wives of men overseas after their husbands were reported missing. The fact that their income is cut down during that time makes it very difficult for them to carry on and pay the cost involved in the birth of a child, as well as meet other obligations they may have entered into.
In view of the hardships thus being suffered by the wives of these men, I suggest that the minister consider this matter, and very soon, in order to rectify what I believe to be a discrimination. I am not the first hon. member to bring this matter before the committee. It has been raised on several occasions before. I commend it to the minister's most serious attention.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext:
Perhaps I should answer at
once the questions of the hon. members for Lambton West and Saskatoon City, so that these questions will not pile up.
First may I say that the air cadets are now to all intents and purposes part and parcel of the Royal Canadian Air Force. We have retained our connection with the air cadet league so that the league might function as a propaganda organization and, with the help of public-spirited citizens, arouse interest in the air cadets. To all intents and purposes we now supervise the work of the air cadet corps, because we consider it one of the most important fields for obtaining recruits in the future, particularly air crew recruits.

Does the department finance
it?

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: Yes-perhaps not entirely, but to a very considerable extent.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
And the
training?

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext:
We are giving them training, too. As a matter of fact that has caused another headache. We are taking them to some of our schools and the question naturally arises whether we will give the boys rides in aeroplanes. Well, if we have 7,000 cadets, as I expect we will have this summer, it would take a good many flying hours to take them up one by one. I suggested to some of our pilots that we might take five or
six at a time in big machines. But one of them said, "Would you like to have a lot of squalling brats crawding all over you in the machine?"-and I said no. As a matter of fact we would have difficulty obtaining permission from parents, and one thing and another; and I believe to take them up in aeroplanes would be too great a risk for us to take. However, all that is by the way.
Now with respect to commissions, I share the views of the hon. member for Lambton West. The situation is that when this air training scheme was inaugurated part of the plan was that 50 per cent of the pilots and observers should obtain commissions. The wireless air gunners were supposed only to become sergeants. It was also arranged that 33 per cent of these commissions were to be granted on graduation, in accordance with the marks attained by the pupil, as in any other school. The other 17 per cent were marked as recommended for promotion.
Well, these lads all went over. Many of them became attached to the Royal Air Force; some of them were in the middle east. We have many hundreds of our men in the middle east. As a matter of fact I have forgotten the figures, but we have a squadron of our own in the far east, and more than one in the middle east, in addition to many hundreds -perhaps thousands-who are connected with the Royal Air Force. The boy who is twenty-first on the list, the twenty preceding him having obtained commissions, may be away off somewhere in Syria. I am sure his commanding officer is not aware of the recommendations made by the commanding officer at Uplands, and I have always felt that that recommendation in many instances was of no value whatsoever. The records do follow the men, in theory; but I doubt if they do in practice.
We had a great deal of difficulty in getting commissions for the 17 per cent who were promised, as part of the plan. Commanding officers in fighter groups, fighter squadrons, bomber groups or bomber squadrons are not apt to worry very much whether Canada has obtained the full 50 per cent of commissions to which it was entitled under the plan. If an individual sergeant is serving in any part of the world his commanding officer may find him to be a good sergeant. But there may be other sergeants of the Royal Air Force who in the opinion of the commanding officer are more worthy of promotion. The officer is not particularly concerned whether Mr. Sergeant, Canadian, comes in under the 17 per cent which would bring the total up to 50 per cent. The result was that for many months we were not getting the quota to which we were



War Appropriation-Air Services
entitled. One of the objects of my visit to Great Britain last year was to insist that somehow or other we be brought up at least to that 50 per cent. It took a long time, but I am glad to say that since December some 350 to 400 of our graduate sergeants have obtained commissions, to bring us up to the 17 per cent. These are rough figures; if required I could put the exact figure on Hansard. However we are away off the total number we should have at the present time.
One of the matters I took up at that time, and which I hope to take up in the forthcoming conference, is the advisability and the absolute justice of making every member of air crew an officer. We are bound at the present time by our undertakings under the joint air training plan. Possibly treasury control in Great Britain has something to do with it, because, as is well known, Great Britain contributes the pay and allowances of the men attached to Royal Air Force squadrons, with the exception that we bring the pay up to the Canadian rate. That means an addition of about one-third more. That may have had something to do with the reluctance of the British treasury to do anything further at the time the plan was inaugurated.
I read in British Hansard-and I believe this appeared in the Winnipeg Free Press-an account of a bomber returning from a raid over Germany. The pilot of the machine was a sergeant while the observer was an officer. They had been together for eighteen to twenty hours and had gone through a veritable hell of flak fire. When they returned the man who brought the machine home walked into the sergeant's mess and the fellow that he had carried home went into the officer's mess. As one labour member in the British house put it, one walked into the players' and the other walked into the gentlemen's room. There is neither rhyme nor reason or common sense about that.
It is a hangover of ia past age.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext:
It may be a treasury matter, but so far as I am concerned it will not be a a treasury matter in Canada. It is one of the matters to be taken up at the forthcoming conference. May I say, in case I have given an unfavourable impression of the feeling of the high command in Great Britain, that I have spoken to some of the highest officers in the Royal Air Force and they are in entire agreement that every member of the air crew should be an officer. It might have been better if we had called them all ensigns or had adopted some kind of intermediate title indicating that they were not
tMr. Power.]
fully graduated as officers in the sense of having gone through an officers' course such as one has to undergo in the infantry or in the artillery. Except in certain instances, they are not taught to lead men. A man who is running his own machine, perhaps a single-seater fighter, may be the finest pilot in the world, but until he becomes a flight commander or squadron leader or wing commander he need not necessarily have the qualities of leadership which may be required in a man who leads, let us say, a platoon or a company of infantry. Nevertheless in a machine they all take the same risks. As the hon. member for Lambton West, has pointed' out, in many instances they left home as buddies, went through the same school, and because of a difference of one or two points, one has to be a gentleman and the other has to be a player. I can assure the committee that we will see that that is not done, if I can help it.
With respect to the many questions asked by the hon. member for Saskatoon City, I may say that of the $344,000,000 in the estimates, some will be required for the construction of additional accommodation. It seems to me that we are always building something or other. Even with the shift that we expect to make, the changing of certain areodromes and schools from one destination to another, this will be necessary. Certain elementary schools will disappear and be replaced by operational training schools. We are extending the scope of our training so that in many instances a man will be fully trained operationally on operational machines. Other schools will be doubled, and some will be tripled. But with all that, I do not visualize any extended programme of building or the establishment of new schools this year. It may be necessary to add two or three schools in order to balance the new set-up, but that I think will be mostly in the way of location of additional aerodromes this year. It must be understood that this refers only to the joint air training plan. We have located- one of the reasons for my recent trip to western Canada was this-a certain number of aerodromes on the Pacific coast and elsewhere in spots where they will be most useful for the defence of the coast. There will be new aerodrome construction on both east and west coasts for defence, but not for air training purposes.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Is consideration being given to the abandonment of other plans? I have heard some statement that perhaps Pennfield Ridge will be abandoned.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext:
Perhaps I am not supposed to say so, but that school was used for astral navigation. In that part of the world they

War 'Appropriation-Air Services
never seem to see the sun, so that we are using it for another purpose, one for which it is well fitted indeed. The climate there is somewhat similar to the climate in certain parts of the old country, and some of the work which has been carried on in the old country can be transferred to Pennfield Ridge.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: I was not thinking of its being abandoned, I was thinking that some change might be contemplated. I hope the committee will not take the minister's statement too literally, that we never see the sun in the county of Charlotte.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: It was the stars I meant. The hon. member for Saskatoon City wanted to know what had become of our reserves. The reserve we have at the moment is probably not very large; I think about 1,000 men are on leave without pay to report at a certain date. We have a considerable number on what we call tarmac duty, which was formerly called guard duty, and on guard duty.
Is that the extent of our reserve?

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext:
At the present time I would say that we probably have three or four months ahead of us. We also have a reserve of those who are undergoing youth training. I think I said there were 1,300 under youth training. Then we have those whose applications have been completed and others whose applications are incomplete. We anticipate no great difficulty in obtaining recruits, certainly for six months. Then based on last year's results a large number of boys will have matriculated from high school and will come in during the summer. Figuring on that, I think we are well away for the next year anyway.
With respect to the number of planes that we have, I believe I committed an indiscretion in stating the number which we should have for training. I am only too willing to renew it by saying we are so close to 6,000 now it is no fun. Spares will always be a problem. Only recently I was speaking to a friend of mine in the army who is closely connected with a munitions assignment in the United States. He tells me that there, as in Great Britain and as in Canada-perhaps it is better now-no matter what it is they wish to procure, whether it be tanks, trucks, guns or rifles, it is difficult to get the manufacturer to make spares. They all want to be able to say that they have turned out so many of such and such an article. I think our spare situation is easier than it was. We are still meeting with difficulties, but there is no chance of our being bogged down now as I felt there was over a year ago.
44561-149i
Are they producing more in this country?

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext:
We are making more and more as time goes on. I was told a year ago that there were certain spares that could not possibly be made in this country. I was informed only a few days ago that they are being made, and made in reasonably large quantities.
With regard to our recruits from those in military camps who have been called up under the mobilization act, the Department of National Defence under an arrangement made a year or so ago, or at all events early in the war, permits us to recruit these men if they have not been with the army for more than two months. At the end of the two months the army says: You have had a chance to get these men for two months, and you have not taken them, so now let us carry on with them. After all, the army has been spending money od them, and it would not be fair for us to take them away from the army after that length of time. We have no arrangement at present for taking men out of the army :n Canada because it does cost the army a lot if money to train the men and it would hardly be fair to allow a man whom the army has trained for six months in some trade to change his mind and come over to us. But we have made arrangements with the Canadian forces overseas to take from the army a certain number who wish to. join the air force. Presumably they did not have the same opportunity of joining the air force in Canada early in the war, when it was almost impossible for many men to get into the air force. So that the men serving overseas with the army, if they so desire, have the opportunity of transferring to the air force.
With regard to pay and allowances of the missing, I was not in the house when my colleague the Minister of National Defence spoke of the different treatment between the army and the air force in regard to members of the forces who are missing, and I use the word "missing" advisedly because they must be declared missing. Furthermore, I do not know of anyone in the army who has been declared "missing" as yet.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: They have not yet got to that stage.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext:
No. I will say this. The British government have the same system as we follow in the air force whereby almost immediately, or at least at the end of the current month, members of the forces who are missing are listed as missing even before they are listed as presumed dead. In our own case, in the air force, I have here a memoran-

War Appropriation-Air Services
dum from the dependents' allowance board which I took the trouble to get-the hon. member for Davenport had asked the question, which I looked up in Hansard, and the ruling of the dependents' allowance board applies to both the army and the air force. Their memorandum is as follows:
When a member of the Royal Canadian Air Force is reported as missing the following procedure is carried out in regard to his pay and dependents' allowance.
(X) Any assigned pay, or assigned pay and dependents' allowance which is in payment is continued to the end of the month in which the casualty is reported and then ceases as such.
(2)	From the end of this month the dependents' allowance board immediately institutes a special temporary allowance to the dependent in an amount not greater than the amount to which the dependent would be entitled as pension if the man were reported as dead. This allowance continues until the fate of the man is definitely decided.
(3)	If the man is reported alive, either as prisoner-of-war interned in a neutral country, or having returned to duty, service pay and dependents' allowance is reinstated retroactively over the period during which he was reported as missing.
(4)	If the man is officially reported as dead pension ruling is immediately given by the pension commission. Arrangements are made so that the allowance paid by the dependents' allowance board ceases as soon as pension is in payment.
(5)	Where assigned pay only, and no dependents' allowance is in payment it is considered prima facie evidence that the recipient of the assigned pay is not dependent on the man and the payment of the assigned pay therefore ceases at the end of th'e month in which the casualty is reported.
(6)	Members of the Royal Canadian Air l'orce who are reported as casualties while serving with the Royal Air Force receive the same treatment, and at the same rates as if they were serving with their own force.
That is the situation with respect to the missing, and from my information. I would say that it applies as well to the. army as to the air force. The situation is this. Hardships may arise, depending on the amount of pay which the man assigns. Let us say that the wife of a pilot or sergeant receives a dependents' allowance of $40 a month-I do not know the exact figure, I think it is $35; but for the sake of illustration we will say $40.-and that the pilot assigns $40 more to her. That makes a total of $80 a month. If he is posted as missing, at the end of the month his wife receives $60 a month, which is the maximum she would receive by way of pension, and of course she loses his assigned pay. So that there is a difference of $20 between the $60 a month she receives when he is missing and the $80 a month she was formerly receiving. The reason for that-I am speaking subject to

the information I received from the dependents' allowance board-is that the board does not want to pile up against the man's wife, in case he should afterwards be declared dead, $20 or $30 or $40 more a month than she would be entitled to by way of pension.
Not if the board would have to ask for it back.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: But the crown would have no right to pay the salary and allowance of a man who was dead, to be quite frank about it. If a man were not posted as missing but was known to be dead, his dependent would go on pension and the presumption of death, I take it, would be retroactive. That would be my interpretation of the regulations after many years of playing around with pension law and regulations in that regard. I know that that is done by the dependents' allowance board, and I would think it the logical if not the sympathetic way of interpreting the regulations. I know it may strike the members of the committee as not being the right thing to do, but I do not know what else could be done unless the house were to vote a certain sum of money to be allocated to dependents of the missing until such time as they were presumed dead.

Paragraph 5 of the memorandum which the minister has just read deals with the cutting off of assigned pay when a man is reported as missing. I have in mind a specific case of that kind. What is the mother to live on until some adjustment is made?

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: It is assumed, I take it, that if the man has not arranged for his mother to receive a dependents' allowance she is not a dependent, and if he does not ask that she shall receive a dependents' allowance the question naturally arises: Should the state do so?

In the particular case I have in mind the man was assigning $50 a month to his mother. He was reported missing on the seventeenth of the month. She received no assigned pay for that month, none for the previous month, and none of his regular pay, and she had nothing to go on with. The man had been assigning $50 a month to his mother, who is a widow, and it should be assumed by the board that he is her support, since his pay, including his assigned pay, was being sent to her.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext:
I am under the impression that in order to establish dependency a man must at least advise the board that his mother is dependent upon him.

War Appropriation-Air Services

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
He has
to apply on. her behalf.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext:
Yes. I get $20 a month
assigned pay from my boy in the Royal Air Force. If I am not mistaken, they are allowed only to send a certain amount of money, and perhaps they send it to their parents in order that their parents can return it to them in pounds. The fact of assignment would not necessarily mean dependency on the part of the parent. If I am not mistaken, a great many young fellows in the air force draw only Royal Air Force rates of pay in England; the pilot's Canadian rate of pay is deferred, and they get the Canadian rate of pay forwarded to their parents and the parents send it back.

But that, as I understand
it, is not permitted unless it is established that the mother is a dependent. As a matter of fact cases have been referred to the Minister of National Defence in which there was a refusal to allow a release of the money because it was not established that the mother was dependent. . Investigations are constantly being made by various associations which are affiliated with the dependents' allowance board to determine whether the mother is dependent and should get this assigned pay.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext:
I do not think that in our
service there is any rule against anybody assigning pay to a relative; I do not know about assigning it to an outsider. If you do not want to attach dependency to it, that is no crime. Perhaps the army rules differ in that respect from ours, because I gather that in the army there is a deferment of pay, that they do not permit the man to receive immediately the entire amount on his arrival here from the other side. So far as we are concerned, when a man comes back from the other side, if he has a credit coming to him he has not much trouble in getting his deferred pay if he wants it; we do not keep it until after the war.

Would the dependents' board acknowledge a power of attorney? I know of a case similar to that mentioned by the hon. member for Fraser Valley. Two boys in the air force assigned portions of their pay to parents who needed the money, but never applied for any other assistance. There was a third boy who has, I believe, become a prisoner of war in Java. A power of attorney was given because the father had had a partial stroke and the lad thought that something more serious might happen to him. The board however refuses to allow the father to cash the cheque under
his power of attorney. They are very independent people, but there is a real need, and it is creating hardship.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext:
I hope I shall not be
brought into a discussion, concerning the dependents' allowance board, which is not my baby, but so far as it relates to the air force, once a man has established dependency I believe the right is admitted. Perhaps conditions are freer and easier in the air force than in the army.

I congratulate the minister
on the sketch he has given us of the work of his department. He assured us that he is a real pilot, that he knows his chart, and that he goes places from which he expects to come back.
There are one or two things I should like to suggest. First, there is the matter of entertainment. Any group of men who are under great strain need to have a bit of good clean fun. I noticed a trainer who had been for a ride, because the recruit was the one who was doing the flying; he came back from about six hours in the air and sat down and just looked at space. These men need the best kind of entertainment so that their vision will be clear and their nerves steady and in such shape that they can stomach anything they may encounter. Therefore I compliment the minister on the splendid entertainment which he has given not only to the air force but to all Canada in sponsoring hockey, here in Ottawa and all over the dominion. Any hockey team which can defeat a team from the head of the lakes, whether Fort William or Port Arthur, must know its stuff. We believe that we at the head of the lakes have the best amateur team in Canada. Instead of being criticized the minister should be commended for taking young men who were formerly professionals and putting them in line again to show the young fellows how to play the game. It is true that they met their match when they ran up against the Bearcats of Port Arthur. This provides entertainment of the right kind, because the boy who is a good athlete and keeps his body and mind in right shape will make a great aviator.
Another thing. There are 422,000 in the volunteer forces of Canada, and if it takes fifteen men to keep one man equipped, it is gong to take about 6,300,000 persons outside of the forces busy to keep those men at the front equipped. Therefore I would ask the minister if he expects to displace a great many men, who are working in the air force,

War Appropriation-Air Services
by young women. They will not have the same risk as the fighting men, and it would free men in the force for other work.
I do not suppose there is one man in this chamber who does not wish to heaven he were on the young side of thirty so that he could take a course as an air pilot. I know that I would like it immensely. Of course some of us will have to go up in the air in other ways. But no one can overestimate the tremendous risks which these young fighters incur. I have been informed by men who have been overseas that a large percentage of those who make the first thirty trips over to Germany do not come back, and less than 11 per cent of those who make the second thirty trips come back. When you think that 89 per cent of those young men will not return, you realize that it is the duty of Canada to uphold in every way possible the hands of the men who are taking to the air and fighting for us. We must see that they are properly equipped in every possible way. I am sure also that the minister will see to it that they have the opportunity of plenty of entertainment and fun and those things which they need to help them to live through their times of quiet.

Further in regard to missing pilots, may I refer to a letter from a lady in Peterborough. She states that her son was in the air force stationed at Gander, Newfoundland, and continues:
Last December 29, 1941, I had a telegram telling me that my dear son was missing. That was December 29 last. I received his allowance on December 30 and have received nothing since. On February 6 I wrote to the officer commanding about his personal belongings, and I happened to mention about the allowance being stopped. I will have to wait six months before Ottawa declares my son dead. They are not sure of his death yet, but they have stopped my allowance.
I understand that if the man had been a prisoner of war the allowance would have kept on, but owing to the fact that he is missing it has stopped. Here is a woman whose husband is seventy. Her son was giving her $20 a month before he left and now that is stopped and they have nothing to live on.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: Assigned pay or allowance?
Assigned pay.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: Not dependents' allowance?
No, assigned pay. These people are absolutely in want.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext:
I have no idea why he did
not make an assignment, why he did not arrange to establish dependency on her part.
I have a letter from her in which she says that she does not think the boy knew how to do it or understood it.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: That would be a case to put before the dependents' allowance board itself. If my hon. friend will send me the letter I shall be glad to see that some of the officers of the department make a claim on the dependents' allowance board and get the law and the prophets on it, whatever it may be.

I join with other members who have commended the minister for the splendid and concise statement he has given the committee. It is indeed in keeping with the two statements already given by the other ministers of national defence who preceded him. Now we have a perfectly clear picture of the defence departments of Canada. Personally I should like to do away with the word "defence". We must have more of the fighting spirit if we are going to win the war. Staying back in Canada and hoping to win the war by merely defending Canada will never bring success to our arms. We must go out and meet the enemy and fight him wherever he can be found. Therefore I would prefer that instead of designating these ministers as ministers of national defence we call them "ministers of war".
I join with the hon. member for Lamb ton West (Mr. Gray) in the suggestion regarding commissions for all men who are part of the air crew. I was very happy indeed to hear the Minister of National Defence for Air say that he also was in sympathy with this suggestion. It is quite natural that he should agree with it; for hon. members will recall that he himself enlisted in the last war as a private and went through the ranks, finally becoming an officer. He does not believe in keeping commissions for the favoured few, and I do hope that the day will soon come when all members of the air crew will be commissioned officers.
There is one class which I hope will receive commissions fairly soon. I refer to the young men who are now in Britain who fly night after night over Germany. In Britain there are officers flying aircraft over Germany and there are also sergeant pilots, sergeant observers and sergeant air gunners. These men risk their lives every time they fly over Germany, and any man who is gallant and courageous enough to fly over that country should be a com-

War Appropriation-Air Services
missioned officer and should be entitled to the very best that this or any other nation can give him. Therefore I suggest that one of the first things the minister should try to do should be to forget the rank with which these men graduated from the air schools in Canada, whether they came first or last, because they are now in England flying over Germany and they should take second place to none; they should all be commissioned officers.
These men who fly over Germany are entitled to the best that can be given them in Britain. It wras my privilege last fall to visit Britain. It was my privilege with five other members of the house to visit certain stations from which men fly over Germany. I recall visiting one of these commands one morning about nine o'clock. Two nights before the men from that command had flown over Germany. Did we find them living in comfort, men who had come back after risking their lives? I do not want to paint a picture of hardship as applying to the conditions under which they live, but I do not believe they are living in the comfort in which they should live after making such hazardous trips. An hon. member who preceded me referred to hockey teams in Canada. I would say without hesitation that the men who play on a hockey team live more or less like kings compared to the men who fly by night over Germany. I do not think that is right. The men who man the aeroplanes should get the very best treatment, the treatment that is given any athlete. They should be treated as our hockey players or baseball players or other athletes are. What do we find however? I recall that visit. It was a rainy morning, dull and cold. We entered a so-called sergeant's hut, not at all comfortably furnished, and there we saw three men huddled around a stove in one comer of the hut with blankets wrapped around them, trying to keep themselves warm. The other members with me on that occasion will recall our comments. We said, "These men are entitled to something better than this." I believe they are entitled to something better than that and I trust that something better can be given them. I trust that the best that can be provided will be theirs.
There is one other matter to which I would refer, namely, the airfields which we have in Canada. We are very happy indeed to have in the neighbourhood of the city of Brantford two airports, and I can only speak in the highest terms of the personnel of those schools. The commanding officers, the officers, the instructors and the young pilots and the ground crew have all established for themselves a place in the hearts of the people of Brantford city and we are indeed happy to have them in
our midst. The air schools are both beyond the limits of the city of Brantford. Let me refer first to No. 4 wireless school in the township of Brantford. As I said, we are glad to have these schools in our midst, but I would point out to the minister that the land on which they are located is exempt from taxation. No. 4 wireless school is in the township of Brantford in school section No. 7. The total number of acres exempt is 374. The total assessment of that school section is $289,900, while the assessment for the land and buildings of the school, which are exempt, is $17,300, or approximately 7 per cent of the total. The tax rate in that section is 2-9 mills, and there is no outstanding debt. The amount lost in taxes is $401.07, or 7 per cent of the total amount of taxes.'
Then the Burford airport, which is also in the township of Brantford and which is known as No. 5 service flying training school, comprises 582 acres, all in school section No. 9. The total assessment of that school section is $340,795; the assessment of the lands and buildings of the school, which are exempt, is $28,400, or approximately 8 per cent. The amount of taxes lost on that airport is $787.65. So that the total amount of taxes lost to the township of Brantford by virtue of these airports is $1,118.72. That does not seem a large amount of money, but in these two school sections it is a fair proportion of the total, amounting to 7 per cent in one case and 8 per cent in the other. Someone has asked what the school sections get out of it. They get very little out of it in dollars. As I said before, they are happy to have these airports located there, but after all an airport does not bring only happiness to a district. It is not a pleasant thing for those in the vicinity of these airports to have aeroplanes flying a few hundred feet over their buildings all day and almost all night.
Better than bombing.

Much better than bombing, and they are very glad to have those airports; let me make myself clear on that. The people in those districts welcome the airports, but I still say it is not the most comfortable thing for those living in the immediate vicinity of these airports to have aeroplanes flying over their houses and buildings all day long, whether they are awake or asleep. As we all know, when these aeroplanes land, they come very close to these buildings. I see some hon. members smiling and laughing, but I ask those hon. members how they would like to sleep in a building adjoining an airport and have aeroplanes flying only a few hundred feet

War Appropriation-Air Services
over their heads day in and day out. And more than that, it is not altogether a pleasant sensation to have the beacon lights flashing in your windows every few seconds all night long, every night of the week. The people are not complaining about having these airports in their districts, but there are two sides to the story. We sit here in comfort. We do not have the aeroplanes, flying over our heads while we are in this building; the lights are not flickering all night long, and we must be fair with the people who live in these districts. I think, as I have said already, that we should express our deep appreciation of the way they have welcomed these airports, in spite of the discomfort that has resulted.
The point I should like to make is that something should be done in regard to the payment of taxes to the townships in which the one hundred airports in Canada are located. It would not amount to very much money for the government- to pay, but every person living in these districts pays taxes; why should not the dominion government also pay taxes on these airport properties? I ask the minister to consider the suggestion. I ask him to consider whether it would not be fair for the dominion government to pay taxes, just as taxes must be paid by any person who happens to live in the township.

I should like to
offer a solution to the minister in this connection. In my riding I have no war industries, and I suppose they have two or three hundred industries in Brantford. If it hurts their feelings to have aeroplanes flying overhead, and if they are too tired to pull down the blinds to keep out the light, you can put all the airports you like in my riding, and we will not care about the $1,188 in taxes.

First I want to thank the minister for having answered a question which I asked some days ago. I believe at the time he was away on some other business, but the fact that he answered my question is just another indication of his meticulous attention to duty.
With the others who have spoken I honour these wonderful young men of the air force, many of whom, including the sons of my three immediate neighbours, have come from my riding. Certainly they have held high the honour of Canada, as the minister has said, on every field of battle throughout the world. I only wish we could double, treble or quadruple our efforts. I am not finding fault with what has been done. I think we have done splendidly; but if we could greatly extend our facilities for training these wonderful 
young Canadian aviators I am sure they would help bring the war to a conclusion in a much shorter time.
Two years ago, and again last year, when this subject was before the house, I said that aeroplanes would either win or lose the war. When we have such wonderful young men in Canada, and when we have plants producing areoplanes, I do not see why we cannot greatly increase our facilities both for training aviators and for making aeroplanes. Only to-day the latest reports indicate that three British destroyers have been sunk in the Mediterranean by axis areoplanes. If we had an abundance, a superabundance, of aeroplanes not only in the Mediterranean but in every other field of battle, our destroyers would not be sunk, nor would the Repulse and Prince of Wales have been lost off Malaya. Both those battleships were sunk because of the lack of air protection. And even more recent than the sinking of the battleships we had the loss of two cruisers, at least one of which had a very distinguished record, having taken part in the sinking of the Graf Spee or the Bismarck. Both these cruisers were sunk through lack of air protection. I am wondering, with all the minister's ability and energy, if he could do more than he has done. Perhaps no one else could have done as much, but it is possible that he could do more to train more aviators here, and also order more planes.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: I am sorry to say we have so far fulfilled our contract that they do not want any more at the present time.

Well, that passes all
comprehension.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: It is not my business.

Whether anybody wants them or not, they should be built. If the British do not want more planes and more aviators, I would feel that some one wants to lose the war, and I cannot conceive that they want to lose the war. I am convinced that they want to win the war, although sometimes it looks as if somebody in behind is 'blocking the winning of the war-but not intentionally; rather it is through something they do not have in their hearts or heads. However, that does not affect the minister.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: No; they got all the pilots they could hold, for the moment.

Let us consider a case in point. Last year the aeroplane factory in the constituency of Fort William, the representative of which spoke a few moments ago, ceased making bombers. That factory was building hurricane bombers. I believe they were turning out about a hundred a month.

War Appropriation-Air Services
They may have been turning those planes out for an English order; I do not know. However, for lack of orders they shut down on bombers, and remained shut down for six or seven months. This means that aeroplane facilities, for both defence and attack, for Great Britain and her allies, are short by six hundred or seven hundred bombers they should have had-and could have had. Those bombers could have been made in Fort William. The plant has now started again producing at the rate of a hundred a month. We are not responsible, of course. I believe that the planes manufactured there were sent to Great Britain. But could we not have taken any extra planes they could supply? Could we not have put them in stock? Could we not have sent them out to the east?
Only recently we have learned that after displaying wonderful valour our troops retreated through Malaya. They retreated three or four hundred miles. We learned that they had to retreat because they had not sufficient air protection. Then, when they retreated out of Malaya into Burma, the same story was told us in the press. We are told now that they have retreated a distance of three or four hundred miles north, up along the Irrawaddy river. What is the reason given? They have not sufficient aeroplane protection.
Somebody is responsible for the fact that British troops everywhere have not sufficient aeroplane protection. If Canada can produce aeroplanes-and we certainly produced the pilots and the air crew-then we should produce them.'
Our young men are thrilled with the story of Bishop and those other Canadians who distinguished themselves so much in the last war, and who so brilliantly electrified Europe with their ability to shoot down our enemies. Canadians could do it again. Why, then, can we not give them the planes-thousands of planes, and air crew in thousands and thousands, so that our brave sailors on the seas will not have their ships sunk from under them through lack of aeroplane protection, and our brave troops on land will not have to retreat because of lack of aeroplane protection.
I am convinced that if the minister were given a carte blanche order to turn out another ten thousand aviators, no matter what the cost, he would do so. I have every confidence in his ability and in the organization of his department to build more training fields, and to turn out any number of aviators required. Then, since we are not to blame, who is to blame for the fact that
everywhere we have not the aeroplane protection we should have?
Something was said a short time ago about repair parts for aeroplanes. Perhaps there is a reason for the shortage along that line. That is not in the minister's department, and I would not criticize the Minister of Munitions and Supply (Mr. Howe) because he, too, has done a splendid job. But somebody, somewhere, is to blame for the whole aeroplane industry not having been producing more. The men at the head of it are big enough to organize it. I know many of them. I have the background of what is behind the fact that they have not been turning out more planes, so I will not criticize anybody. But the fact is that they could do infinitely more. Why, Canadian plants did not get into really high speed until after Japan came into the war. Between the time of the outbreak of war and the fall of France our aeroplane companies were running, I presume, at about 20 per cent capacity, and between the fall of France and the advent of Japan in the war they were turning out not more than 75 per cent, at the outside.
So I should hope that through the minister's energy and ability something will come about whereby Canada will produce thousands more planes and thousands more crews to man those planes. If that happens, the war will end just that much more quickly.
I should like to thank the minister for a reply he gave me yesterday in writing. I had received a long wire from Drumheller, a place I visited last summer. It is a very beautiful town in Alberta, in fact one of the most beautiful I have been in. It is a town to which I would recommend anyone who travels to the west to visit. In that vicinity are great resources of coal. The wire intimated that if the government intended extending the building of fields in the west, Drumheller might be considered. In that vicinity they produce about a million and a half tons of coal a year. I am happy to say that a large proportion of that coal comes to Ontario, and I hope much more of it will come here. In the production of that coal there is a great deal of slack. While out there I learned with keen interest how cheaply they can produce power from their slack coal. Therefore, if the minister in future extends air facilities in the west, I would submit he should consider the vicinity of Drumheller as a place where he could have an air field. The cheap light and power would be one inducement, I should think, and the vast abundance of coal in the vicinity would be another.

War Appropriation-Air Services

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: Will I send the hon. member for Brantford City to Drumheller to explain ;he disadvantages?

My suggestion is a
fair one, since the hon. member for Brantford City is not altogether too pleased with all that is happening in Brant county. If you do happen to move them out of the county of Brant, you might put one or two in the county of York. We have quite a number, but we could take one more. Then you could send some of the surplus ones out to Drumheller.
I stated that the county of Brant was very happy to have these air ports in its midst.

I know it is. I know the county of Brant pretty well.
I happened to come across a number of complaints yesterday. It may be that they are not worth while talking about, but if they are real complaints I know the minister will take steps to clean them up. A father told me a few days ago about his boy, who had enlisted in the air force. At two camps, and perhaps a third one, the boy had been acting as guard, and had been doing scrubbing, and work of that kind. This boy graduated as a senior matriculant. Perhaps in passing I might mention that he is an only son, although I realize, of course, that that point has no particular bearing. I have known this boy quite well, and in my opinion he is a bright young man. The father came to see me and pointed out his distress at the fact that after being in the Royal Canadian Air Force that length of time the boy had not been posted to anything other than scrubbing or guard duty. Of course, that may be part of the training; I do not know. If it is, then all right. But if there is such a surplus of young men around air training camps, there should not be. Certainly there should not be a surplus so great that they have to be put at scrubbing, cleaning and guard duty. They should be thoroughly trained and trained as quickly as posible so that they can get into the work for which they have joined the army.
I should like to know how men in the Royal Canadian Air Force are posted to the Royal Air Force. I have in mind a young man who recently went overseas as an aviator -perhaps this is the case to which the minister referred a short time ago-and was in England only a short time when he was sent to the Royal Air Force in Gibraltar. The next day he was in Malta and the next day he was shot down. The question is whether 
or not he was thoroughly trained to go on a bombing expedition of that kind. Are our men trained sufficiently in Canada so that when they reach England they can go immediately on bombing expeditions? Do we plan to train our men in Canada to the same extent as our cousins to the south do? When their men leave the United States they are evidently trained 100 per cent and can go into action immediately, as they demonstrated with such daring over the Coral sea during the last few days.
I have just one further point to raise. A few days ago the picture of a hockey coach appeared in our papers. I shall not give the name of this man, but he had1 been quite active in sports, about which I know very little. It may have been thought desirable that such men should be kept physically fit, but the fact is that when he was sent to the air training camp he was posted immediately to the administrative department. The father of a boy in the same camp wrote me a letter inquiring why his son who had been there for a long time and had applied on various occasions for a promotion to some administrative post could not get that promotion whereas this coach was immediately placed in an apparently preferred position. I wonder if every one who joins the air force is treated exactly the same? I hope later on, when the Minister of Munitions and Supply is before us, to try to work out some way so that the minister may have ten planes for every one he has now? I heard him say in the course of his remarks that he has more men trained for the air than there are planes in which to put them.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: On the other side.

In Great Britain, but
not here. That bears out a remark I heard when I was in an aeroplane plant a short time ago. They told me that they had1 more planes here than we had men to man them.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext:
I did not say that. I said
that our output has been more than sufficient to meet all the requirements we undertook to meet on the other side, so much so that there is a surplus. That is where we want our men.

A conference is to take
place later on this month between the heads of the air forces of the allies. I should like to see some arrangement made whereby they can collectively produce planes more rapidly and in greater numbers than is being done to-day, and at the same time train crews for those planes so that in the not long distant future the skies above Germany will be black with British planes and the skies above Russia

War Appropriation-Air Services
will also be black with British planes supporting our ally. Throughout the world, in Libya, in the Mediterranean, in Bengal, in the Coral sea, in Australia and elsewhere we must have clouds of planes in the skies to act against the enemy and to support our ships and our men on land.

This is the third arm of Canada's defence service which has presented its report, and I think it is only right that a tribute should be paid to the men- who yesterday sat in our high schools and played on our ball fields but who are to-day flying the fortresses and combat planes in the skies wherever the allied forces are meeting the enemy. Canada's achievements in connection with each one of her armed forces are the object of pride to the Canadian people. I think Canada is particularly proud of her air force. One feature of the air force which warrants considerable tribute is the fact that it has been able to adapt itself to rapidly changing technique. Anyone following developments realizes that as bombing tactics are changed, as the effects from bombing are found out from bitter experience, as the form of fighting changes, rapid changes must be made in training, in the arming of aeroplanes and in the construction of aeroplanes. I think the Canadian air force and the Department of National Defence for Air deserve a tribute for what has been done in this connection.
It must have been satisfying to all of us to hear the minister state that we are now sending men to Britain in numbers sufficient to equal any demand that she may make. Almost every hon. member knows scores of lads of yesterday who are now fighting, or who have paid the supreme sacrifice. It was also with considerable satisfaction that we learned from the minister that he has plans for expanding the air training scheme and that the expenditures for this arm of the service are to be expanded this year.
When the records are tabled covering the number of flying hours put in, I think it will be found that the western provinces have proved to be particularly suitable for elementary training. This is due to the clear skies and the type of terrain which are to be found in that part of the country. It is hoped that the airfields in the west will be expanded in order to meet any further commitments. The record of the commonwealth air training scheme is one of which we can feel justly proud. One thing that mars it in my opinion is the fact that there appear to be almost limitless expenditures in order to get the job done. At times it seems to me that there is a wasteful procedure in connection with certain phases. When the minister was making
his statement last year he told us that they had had to pay rather high prices for materials and services because they wanted aerodromes and other services constructed with the greatest possible speed.
I had a return brought down in the house a short time ago, and I was rather sorry to learn from it that there is no departmental repair depot for engines in Quebec, that some private concern was doing this repair work for Quebec and parts of Ontario. It is to be hoped that private enterprise is not to enter to too great an extent into the services in connection with our armed forces. I was pleased to hear the minister state this afternoon that they are going to take away the elementary training schools from private companies.
