With regard to training air crew, I am sure that it has been of inestimable value to have a large staff of British officers come over to Canada to assist in the setting up of the plan, but I hope that as soon as possible the minister will take advantage of the opportunity to replace them by trained Canadians who have had experience in actual combat, and in control work, in administration, in training and instruction in the old country and in various theatres of war. The minister stated this afternoon that he thought the treasury board had probably as much to do with it as anybody that he was restrained from carrying out the policy of granting commissions practically to everyone who was trained in Canada to fly.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: Not our treasury board, but the British treasury board.

I am referring to the British treasury board, and I should like to have a statement from the minister showing to what extent the British treasury board does exercise control over here, over the policy of his department and administration, and the precise nature of that control.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: They do not exercise control over my department. They pay these pilots when they get overseas, and they do not want to pay out officer's pay when they can get a man as a sergeant. These men are handed over to the Royal Air Force when they get over there.
But the minister said that in his opinion every member of an air crew should have a commission.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: Certainly.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext:
Not under the agreement made in 1939, whereby only 50 per cent could be granted commissions. That agreement was made between the four partners in the deal.
I had nothing to do with that.
Those were the details I wanted. I wanted to know to what extent the minister was prevented from carrying out policies that he thought would be advantageous.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: Read the agreement.

The Minister of
National Defence for Air is one minister who invariably commands the attention of the house and of the committee because when he refers to what is being done in the air he invariably says "Canada" is doing this or that, for which "Canada" should1 be proud, instead of referring to the great efforts that have been made as if they were a party or partisan affair. As I listened1 to his magnificent peroration this afternoon, to his outline of activities of his department and to his plea to the members of this house for an armistice on political partisanship during the period in which the united nations air conference is to meet in Ottawa, it seemed to me that the arguments he advanced in that behalf were equally applicable to times when the air conference is not meeting, and they constituted a very fine commendation of the necessity for a national effort in Canada to-day by a government divorced from political or partisan considerations whose one aim would be victory on behalf of the empire.
There are two or three matters I would bring to the minister's attention. He very frankly agreed with the contention of the hon. member for Lambton West that airmen who have won their wings in the air force should receive commissions. I think that would do very much toward improving the attitude of the men serving to-day in the air force. A few days ago en route to Ottawa I talked with a number of Australians. They have the same system, of course, under the British commonwealth scheme that we have. They mentioned an instance such as was portrayed in the house this afternoon, of the return, of our men after flying over Germany, and then the sergeants going to their mess and the officers to theirs. They said that a new scheme had

War Appropriation-Air Services
been adopted in the Royal Australian Air Force in the east whereby,, instead of having an officers' mess and a non-commissioned officers' mess, officers and men met together in what is known as an air crew mess. I think _ the adoption here of such a scheme would do much to improve morale. It is hard sometimes to see young men, friends through collegiate, friends through university, taking their courses as airmen to be together, followed on graduation by separation, some becoming officers and others non-commissioned officers.
When officers take to the air they get, I understand, $2 a day flying pay, whereas noncommissioned officers who take to the air receive only SI. Is there any reason why officers and non-commissioned officers over Germany or anywhere else, doing identical wrork, should receive any difference in compensation as flying pay? I suggest that if it is impossible under the British commonwealth scheme to make all the crews who have earned their wings commissioned officers, at least the discrimination, if I may call it such, as far as flying pay is concerned, should be done away with.
There is one other matter to which I should like to refer. The hon. member for Yorkton spoke of elementary training schools, to which the minister replied, and rightly, that there is no profit other than 5 per cent paid to those who contribute as shareholders to the establishment of elementary flying training schools. But that is not the position of affairs in air observer schools, which are set up, managed, and operated in various parts of Canada by civilian companies. The elementary schools, with I believe three exceptions, are sponsored by flying clubs. The distribution of profits earned in the operation of elementary flying training schools is that, after 5 per cent is paid to the shareholders-generally members of flying clubs-the remainder is set aside in a common fund and at the conclusion of the contract or of the war will be turned over to the flying clubs setting up the respective schools. That is not so in the case of the air observer schools.
Under the contracts which were made between the government and the air observer schools there was provision for a profit of SI per flying hour. Recommendations were made by the committee on national war expenditures for a reduction of that profit to 35 cents. Would the minister explain whether when, I believe on April 1 of this year, new contracts were drawn with the air observer schools, an alteration was made in the provision relating to profit as far as profit per flying hour is concerned.
There are at the present time-I speak subject to correction-about ten air observer schools in Canada. These schools, set up and constituted for the purpose of training observers and air crew, are owned by private corporations, and there are no controls on the profits which the private companies operating these schools may earn. The position is that they receive a very large amount per month as management fees, and in addition, at the conclusion of the contract they receive 25 per cent of the saving upon maintenance provided for in the target price as set by the department. Be it also noted that these air observer schools are situate in the most strategic parts of Canada. When this war is over there will necessarily be a tremendous expansion of civilian air transportation. It is of great significance to know in whose control these air observer schools are. To-day, if I understand aright, none of them is owned by the Canadian National Railways, but several are owned by the Canadian Pacific railway or its subsidiaries-

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence

-and I think it is only fair that, if a system of private ownership is to continue, some of these should be turned over to the Canadian National Railways, or that railway should be given an opportunity to operate them, so that when the war is over, control of civil aviation will not be exclusively in the hands of one corporation. I have no criticism to offer of the operation of these six schools by the Canadian Pacific railway, but there should be provision made now that when hostilities end, the entire control and maintenance of civil aviation in Canada should not be vested in one transportation corporation. I wish now to ask a series of questions of the minister which, I trust, will clear up the situation as far as these schools are concerned.

the cost per pupil intake was $1,650 while the actual cost to the crown at the present time is SI,075. The operating efficiency of all these . schools is of a high standard, both as to training and as to maintenance of property and equipment, as well as from the economical point of view.
As regards the six companies operated by the Canadian Pacific, and the question as to why the Canadian National does not operate any, my hon. friend will remember that when these contracts were given out-if I remember rightly it was in 1940-a large number of these independent companies had not as yet been absorbed by the Canadian Pacific Railway. The Canadian Pacific, as I recollect, came into the airways field only after these companies had obtained their contracts. Some of the companies are the Yukon Southern and Prairie Airways. I do not know whether it has a contract or not. At any rate, there are six such companies, so that in so far as the Royal Canadian Air Force is concerned it is not our fault if the Canadian Pacific happens to be in a strategic position with respect to airline traffic after the war. I do not know, because I was not in the department at the time, whether T.C.A. was offered contracts, but I presume it was not, because most of these companies were at that time independent; these independent companies were naturally anxious to get into this field, and the department was anxious to have them since they had at their disposal at that time a comparatively large number of trained pilots. It is true that since the plan has been expanded, the pilots as a rule are men who are trained by ourselves, so that what we get mostly is management, knowledge of maintenance, knowledge of the way in which to run aircraft, in perhaps a more efficient manner than would be possible if we did it ourselves. So much have the Royal Air Force been impressed with the work done by civilian companies that they have asked many of these companies to take over the proposed R.A.F. schools in Canada on the same basis as the J.A.T.P. are operated at the present time. Mr. Chairman, just before six o'clock the hon. member for Lake Centre returned to his attack on the air observer schools, in respect of their profits and in respect of the fact that they are being operated by civilian companies. I think the time has come when these attacks, which I consider rather unfair, should be answered.
The committee will recall that the whole question of civilian operated air training schools, that is elementary flying training schools and air observer schools, was referred to the war expenditures committee, which in turn passed on that part of its work to subcommittee No. 1. As chairman of that subcommittee I think I should remind the hon. member and the committee of a few of the facts. His first charge or attack was that these schools are being operated by private companies, and his contention was that they should be operated by the service. I should like to remind my hon. friend that he was a member of subcommittee No. 1, which on June 2 last 'brought in a unanimous report, in which the hon. member himself concurred. I should like to read what that subcommittee had to say with regard to the fact that these air observer schools are being operated by privately owned companies:
The training command of the Royal Canadian Air Force express their complete satisfaction in the training results of the elementary flying training schools and the air observer schools operated by civilian companies, and they stated any attempt to place the responsibility of this type of training upon schools operated by the service would place "an intolerable burden on the service", in which statement the committee concurs. The committee recommends that we should continue to take advantage of the services of these civilian flying companies, and that the services rendered by them be extended to their full capacity.

War Appropriation-Air Services
Up to that time the subcommittee had not had an opportunity to look into the profits being made by the air observer schools, but the committee continued its studies during the summer months and as a result brought in a further report with respect to air observer schools. I should like to remind my hon. friend of part of the contents of that report, first as to the efficiency of the operation of the schools:
The subcommittee finds that the air observer training schools are being very efficiently managed. The operating cost was originally estimated at $1,653.57 per pupil. The actual operating cost as of March 31, 1941, is $1,001.27 per pupil. With something over ten million miles flown to date these schools have had no casualties of either trainees or operating personnel.
That is truly a remarkable record, I submit, and one which could not have been attained except under the most efficient management.
Then my hon. friend complains of the size of the profits which were being made by the air observer schools, and of the fact that those profits were being earned by civilian shareholders. As he well knows, the whole question of profits was thoroughly gone into >y the committee, and in this connection I should like to read another short extract from the report:
The subcommittee has carefully considered the question of profits which will be earned by the operating companies. Partly on account of highly efficient management and partly on account of the pupil intake as fixed by the contract being increased without proportionate increase in management costs it was found that substantial profits were being earned. The following examples of lunar monthly profits from one of the schools show an average profit of $1,112. . . . This would indicate a yearly profit from that school under favourable conditions of $14,456. In this instance the profit is being earned by private individuals and while the contract restricts the declaration of dividends to 5 per cent annually yet at the conclusion of the contracts there would then be a distribution of accumulated profits. The subcommittee fully appreciates the fact that the air observer schools are being very efficiently managed and that these schools are performing an important war task and also appreciates the fact that measures of economy should not be permitted to slow up our war effort but as the actual circumstances have altered sharply since the contract was first entered into the subcommittee decided that a conference should be called of executive officers representing all of the schools, that the facts should be frankly placed before them and their cooperation invited. The conference was held on June 4 and as a result the operating companies have all voluntarily offered to agree to a reduction of what is described in the agreement as flying hour profits from $1 per flying hour to 35 cents per flying hour.
That was a voluntary effort by the operating companies.

The subcommittee recommends that the contracts should be amended accordingly and expresses its appreciation for this commendable attitude on their part. The subcommittee fully appreciates the fact that even after this reduction in profits is made, efficiently operated training companies will still earn net profits of approximately $5,000 annually after payment of taxes at existing rates, but believes that under the special circumstances surrounding these training agreements the recognized yardstick of measuring profits by their relation to capital employed is not an accurate system to use. In this instance the department is not purchasing goods or commodities but, on the contrary, is purchasing skill and experience. As to all existing professions, tariffs of fees have been established by practice but there are no tariffs available to guide your subcommittee in reaching a correct decision with respect to the present problem. In the light of all the surrounding circumstances the proposed change will satisfactorily meet this problem.
In view of the fact that these operating companies came to the committee voluntarily and offered to reduoe their profits to the point where they would earn only $5,000 annually, for all of their services, I do suggest to my hon. friend that these continuous attacks on civilian owned companies, which are doing such a wonderful war task, should cease.

In the last war the headquarters of the Royal Air Force were in Toronto; there was no Royal Canadian Air Force then in Canada, and during the course of that war over 16,000 air cadets and mechanics were trained. This training was carried on with headquarters at Toronto and suburbs and at camps at Leaside, Armour Heights, Camp Borden, Beamsville, Trenton and many other places. The headquarters of No. 4 school of military aeronautics was at the university of Toronto and affiliated colleges, and the city which supplied and gave all their buildings and grounds and affiliated colleges. Some very fine pilots were turned out. Among those who were trained there were a large number of young Americans, many of them from United States universities and from California and the other Pacific coast states.
Those air men, when they went home, did not do like the Canadian people did. They did not forget all about the war, the air and all that kind of thing. They went into commercial aviation business, with the result that when the Chamberlain government announced its programme of aeroplane development and rearmament a few of these persons in commercial aviation got large contracts. I must say that Colonel Barker, V.C., Colonel Collishaw, M.C., D.S.O., the present Air Marshal Bishop, V.C., and another one named Frank McGill, now air commander at Trenton, urged the authorities of the day to continue

War Appropriation-Air Services
aviation in a commercial way, and also by way of rearmament. But very little was done until shortly after this war broke out, because the pacifists seemed to have control of almost everybody in Canada.
Even some of the school boards abolished the cadet movement, which has always been the backbone of the three arms of his majesty's forces in recruiting. In London, England, the present home secretary, Mr. Morrison, as head of the London county council, refused to give the use of one of the schools in the evening to the Royal Air Force, or allow Jellicoe's speech to be distributed. The same thing happened in Canada. It happened in Glasgow, where they would not allow signs to be put up in street-cars, for air force and army recruiting, because the pacifists reigned.
In 1939 a first return was presented to the house showing the numbers in the army, the navy and the air force, asked for by me before the war. That return, dated April 24, 1939, showed that the Royal Canadian Air Force was composed of only 257 officers and 1,927 airmen. A return was placed on the table two weeks ago and, if the minister would be good enough to look into it, I should like to have it placed on Hansard. It shows the pay and allowances, and other emoluments of the officers and men of all ranks in the air force. The Minister of National Defence supplied this return at my request on an order of the house for all the services, and a number of hon. members have asked for a copy of the air part of the return. I should like now to hand it to the minister to have it checked up, and to see if it can be placed on Hansard, as has been done on occasions by the Minister of National Defence and for the women's army. When war broke out I had a resolution on the order paper, and the, return, No. 44, came down for all his majesty's forces and the women's army on March 24, 1942.

Since war broke out I have had a resolution on the order paper asking for better allowances and better protection to the men of his majesty's forces and Canada's soldiers, including the air force, and asking specially for a system of life insurance on all soldiers, so that they will be taken care of after leaving the forces at the conclusion of the war and for sickness and unemployment insurance. I hope that some effort will be made to carry

War Appropriation-Air Services
these suggestions into effect, and that special consideration will be given to supplies to the air force.
Before the war broke out, municipal, provincial and federal authorities had spent nearly a billion dollars on the dole, during the period of depression and unemployment. In the years 1936, 1937 and 1938 I urged on the government on my motion as a private member that it should adopt a system whereby young people out of high schools would in an apprenticeship system of three years learn military drill, get pocket money, clothing, lodging and deferred pay by signing up for from three to five years and work as apprentices in industry or mechanics in eight or nine key industries. If that had been adopted we would have had about 25,000 skilled mechanics from these industries when war broke out and nearly that number of air mechanics. I am sorry it was not adopted. The money was spent, anyway, on the dole and wasted, and when the war came we found that we were away behind in our preparations.
Many of our young Canadians were overseas a year or two before the war. Some of them had to go at their own expense or on cattle boats to enlist, and that matter has been discussed here. There was some discussion as to whether we should send them over a year before we took part in the war, at Canada's expense, for the Royal Air Force. I know of one young man at Belleville who was helped out of gaol on my request by the Minister of Pensions and National Health. The young man told the magistrate at Belleville that he was sixteen when, in fact, he was only fourteen. The minister interested himself in the young man, and he was released. He was only fourteen, but gave his age as sixteen or seventeen so that he could go overseas in a cattle ship to the old country in order to serve.
I have been pleased to see the work done in connection with cadet services. The school boards of this country deserve a great deal of credit. Long before the South African war, in fact after the Fenian raids, school boards and boards of education supported the cadet movement in the schools of Canada. That movement was the backbone of the militia in the last two generations; it is the backbone of the reserve army, air force and the naval cadets to-day. Boards of education in Canada have done good work in that connection.
I was sony that five or six years ago parliament struck out the vote for the cadet movement. As I have said to some hon. members, I think it would have been far better if the government had left the air force the way it was; that is, actively connected with the army

and the navy, through the school boards. In that way I think we would have had a unified cadet system under public control. True, some say that private citizens and organizations furnish equipment. That may be so, but cadet air services receive, I believe, a $25,000 grant.
One of the most ardent workers in connection with air cadet training has been Right Reverend Bishop Robert J. Renison, of St. Paul's Anglican church, Toronto, a veteran of the great war. I believe that at the annual air cadet service there were 1,200 of all cadet denominations at his church. He was a leader in education and military matters. His son went to the old country in 1938, at his own expense, and joined the Royal Air Force in England. He was a young varsity student and is now a prisoner of war in Bonn. The bishop, one of Toronto's leading citizens, has done a great deal of work in connection with the air cadet services. His other son is with the 48th battalion in England.
A return was brought down in the British parliament in connection with the help given by the women's army, as far as the air service is concerned. I believe that in the pay service, and in many other occupations they could be used to displace some of those between the ages of seventeen and forty-five and release some for overseas and home defence.
An air force return was brought down by the minister, No. 29, on February 26, 1941, with reference to sickness in the manning pool at Toronto. It seemed that the air force got the horse palace and cattle stable buildings there, good modern brick buildings, and the return states that in one there were 864 cases of respiratory throat trouble as well as many other illnesses. Now that the government has taken over this property, on which $23,000,000 had been spent on grounds, buildings and permanent exhibits by the city, the air force should get better equipment and buildings on these grounds like the navy have, and better than they have in connection with the present manning pool.
The empire training scheme has been commented on very favourably many times. Complaints have been made, and I know the minister is doing everything he can in connection with them, about the accommodation on Canadian trains as well as on boats in the ocean service. The minister has been most sympathetic toward these complaints and I know he is doing everything to have an improvement made in better transit accommodation and cheaper meals and all along the line, and as to fares my bill asks for free fares.

I should like to say a word about the losses and deaths in training that have occurred in the air. Of course these losses cannot be compared with the loss of life occasioned by the motor car. In the city from which I come 107 people were killed last year in motor car accidents, and the losses all over Canada from motor cars are most appalling. When a loss of life occurs in connection with the air training scheme I think a copy of the evidence taken at the inquest should be made available to the relatives. These inquests are not civil inquests; they are military inquiries carried on under the regulations of the department. Civil inquests are in public. I have no complaint to make, but the families should have a copy of the evidence and findings and I would offer the suggestion that greater care should be taken to prevent accidents to young pilots in the Royal Canadian Air Force.
I know the authorities have been careful and that accidents are likely to happen when we have such a large number of camps spread all across the country, with a great variety of climatic conditions, but I think every care should be taken. Many of these young men come from other empire countries such as New Zealand and Australia and the most extreme care should be taken. These young pilots are placed in positions of responsibility and accidents will happen. I realize it is not fair to draw rash conclusions; we must compare our losses now with those that occurred in the last war and take into consideration the hours of flying, miles travelled, and so on. Everybody admires these young pilots who fly the skies after a great deal of training, after weeks and months of study. While some of them have the necessary skill, many of them do not have the confidence they should have. The government should see that the camps have the best equipment available, and have rigid inspection of pilots, equipment, and over flights.
I hope that great care will be taken to prevent accidents. We should take into consideration, not only the climate but the position of the camps. I understand from what the minister said last session that he does not locate these camps, that that is done by the Minister of Munitions and Supply. In the case of some of these camps great difficulty has been encountered in getting sewers, water and transportation facilities. Some of the camps in the west and in other parts of the country are not located where they should be. The climate and weather conditions are important factors. Many of these young men who come to this country are not used to our fogs and prevailing climatic conditions, and they may not have as good judgment for distances in
War Appropriation-Air Services
bad Canadian winter weather and other matters as they should have. Referring to this question of accidents in the British House of Commons, Captain Balfour, joint undersecretary for air, said the other day in the house on a discussion of this very matter of air training:
I was very glad indeed that the hon. gentleman raised the question of accidents, because one of the tragic aspects of the administration of a service department such as the air ministry, which my right hon. friend and myself have to face, is that the air, even in peace time, has always taken its toll of human life and that in war the toll is much greater. I can assure him that we regard accidents as incidents which must be investigated and sifted to the uttermost. We are always anxious about accidents; we can never be happy or complacent or satisfied so long as accidents, which might possibly be avoided, occur. We have a complete accidents branch; we sift out statistics of all accidents with a view to finding out whether a particular type of aeroplane is more prone to accidents than to others and whether a particular age group is inclined to be more prone to accidents than another; we study meteorological conditions and get a series of cross sections of all the circumstances attending accidents.
A member inquired about the operational work being carried out with monoplanes, and Captain Balfour replied:
I will gladly answer that point. Biplanes are used to any extent in the training of pilots, only at the elementary stage, and at this stage the biplane has been found to be satisfactory and economical in use. It is our experience that pilots receiving their initial training on biplanes show no variation in skill, as compared with pilots who have received elementary training on monoplane types. I cannot agree that the biplane is inefficient or wasteful, or is not giving our young men a fair chance. On the other hand, the biplane lias not got all the modern developments associated with the low-wing monoplane.
I am satisfied that here in Canada a great deal of care is being taken but, when accidents do occur, I think the parents should be informed immediately and be provided with a copy of the evidence taken before the military court.and its finding. I am sorry that the universities of this country have not received more support from the government in their air programmes and syllabus. The technical school at Toronto applied for a new wing, but their request was not granted. They have been doing a great deal of work in training students, both in the day time and in the night time, in order to qualify them to work in munitions plants and other plants manufacturing aeroplane equipment and all that kind of thing. I believe something should be done to help them because it is essential war work of the greatest national value for total
war.

War Appropriation-Air Services
Have any experiments been carried out, either by the government or by the Canadian National Railways, in connection with the use of air ambulances? These flying schools are located all over Canada, and I am sure that many lives could be saved if we had a proper system of aeroplane hospital ambulances and nursing services. I think this is worthy of immediate consideration. When this war began there were some cardinal errors made in connection with lack of bases and protection of the air force and their aerodromes overseas. Britain was not ready. The pacifists in government were to blame. There are three elements which have caused a heavy loss of life in the air in this war by our naval disarmament. I refer to the reduction in our cruiser strength from seventy, to fifty by the Washington treaty, which reduction was contrary to all Admiralty advice. This has led to great losses of life in connection with flying. Then there was the limitation of our destroyer flotillas on the incorrect assumption that flotilla strength should be determined by the submarine strength of the other powers. Also there was the abandonment of the bases in Ireland. All these have caused a considerable loss of life in connection with the battle of the Atlantic on land, sea and in the air.
Canada should study the effect of the development of the air arm in the conduct of war at sea. We might have some statement about that. After two and a half years of war it should be possible' for this country properly to value and assess the part that air warfare has played so far in this war and what is expected of it to the war's end. It has had some successes in this war and some failures, some successes which were least expected and some failures where success was anticipated. To-night we hear of an enemy submarine sinking a freighter in the St. Lawrence. The enemy is at our front, side, and back doors.
We can learn lessons from the bombing of Britain. Blackouts, per se, are of little value alone. In the daylight attacks on Britain the enemy were favoured by good long-range conditions and by having a ring of bases all round Britain from which their bombers could attack the island, and industries and dense population all together, but the British people withstood the attack. The daylight bombing was a failure. The combination of the Royal Air Force fighters and the antiaircraft guns broke up the daylight attacks. The guns broke up the German formations, and the fighters of the Royal Air Force concentrated on the scattered enemy units. That was responsible for the wide difference

in the figures of losses given out by the Germans and the British. At night the only defence Great Britain had at first against attack from the air was the barrage balloons, which prevented dive-bombing on moonlit nights by the German air force. At first neither the British anti-aircraft guns nor the fighters were effective against the German bombers at night. There were two main reasons why all the cities of Britain did not suffer the fate of Coventry. First, the enemy did not have sufficient heavy long-range bombers available, and there was, secondly, difficulty in routing their formations flying at high speed on dark nights and bad weather from widely separated bases. But the night bombing by the German air force was overcome in time through defence improvements and the British defence of radio location, together with anti-aircraft gunnery. The May blitz on London was the worst, and it was also the most costly for the attackers, and in the result the invasion in the air was on the whole a failure, though a lot of lives were lost and there was heavy civil damage.
I appreciate what has been done in the commonwealth air training plan. The type of recruit offered is most excellent, and we have had no difficulty in getting recruits for the air force as well as for the navy, under the voluntary system. If the proper methods had been adopted from the very beginning of the war, there would have been no difficulty in getting recruits for the army and under voluntary recruiting I think a million men could have been obtained, but as I said when the war started it was almost as difficult to get into the army as it was to get into the Rideau club, which is supposed to have a long waiting list. The policy at that time in getting recruits for the army was on-again, off-again, on-again. If we had had a better system, I believe we would have got the recruits. The military authorities did all they could, and I am not criticizing them at all, far from it, because they are a very fine body of men, and in that tribute I would include the three good ministers of the war departments of his majesty's forces and the Minister of Pensions and National Health, who are all experienced, trained soldiers. I still say, however, that if we had had a proper system of voluntary recruiting for the army at the start we would have done very much better than we did.

Mr. Chairman, I am not in the habit of taking up very much of the time of the house, but some three years ago an airport was started in New Glasgow and the town was asked to buy a large tract of land, which it did and deeded the same to the

War Appropriation-Air Services
government. At that time the government spent in the vicinity of $20,000 in levelling off this field and putting it in shape for hard surfacing. In the last four months four planes have crashed in this vicinity, one at Lismore, which plane was damaged considerably. One landed at the airport and stuck in the mud; another one landed to help it, and I understand that they are both there yet. Three weeks ago another one crashed at the Allan shaft within two miles and a half of the present airport. If this airport had been in condition these planes probably could have landed safely at it.
The damage done to the first plane at Lismore would have more than paid for the hard surfaces of this airport. Planes are flying over New Glasgow night and day. Not having an airport to land at when they are in trouble they may crash, as occurred in the instances of which I have spoken, and at any time there may be loss of life.
I want to read a few paragraphs from a letter I received from Mr. L. D. Payzant, chairman of the airport committee of the New Glasgow board of trade. He says:
Since writing you the above letters, disaster has taken place to three more planes in this area, largely I believe due to the fact that the government have no adequate airport here which means that they did not implement their contract signed with the town of New Glasgow on March 1, 1940.
The additional accidents to which I refer are, I think, familiar to you. Several weeks ago a plane landed on the airport, which of course lacks hard-surfacing, and in the muddy condition of our spring it was injured. A second plane came to its rescue and was likewise mired in the mud, and so far as I know both planes are still there awaiting weather that will dry up the surface of this field. Such a situation is really pathetic when a few thousand dollars would have put the field in shape for emergency use.
On Saturday last another disaster took place. A military plane had to make a forced landing at the back mines just about three miles from our air field which, of course, he probably did not recognize as there are no markings on it whatsoever and no record in the manual supplied to flyers. If the difficulty to planes mentioned herein and those referred to in my letter of January 12 continue, and they are likely to do so as flying around this district seems necessary, it seems the height of folly on the part of the department to ignore the contract with the town. All we are asking for at the present time is to have this field hardsurfaced and made available for planes in emergency.
I submit that for the minister's consideration.

First of all, I should
like to congratulate the Minister of National Defence for Air upon one particular phase of the excellence of the joint air training plan, and that is that I have never at any time
heard any complaints in any way, shape or form that the slightest tinge of politics was mixed up with this magnificent plan.
There are one or two suggestions I wish to make, possibly from a military point of view. It has been my privilege to discuss the campaign in Libya not only with air force officers but also with army officers and with United States observers of that campaign. Nearly all of them have said this one thing, that a break-down was caused by lack of cooperation between the two forces, the air and the army. They simply did not think in terms of each other's weapons.
I suggest to the minister that here we have a great air training scheme, as well as a military training scheme, and eventually the army and the air force will have to fight together. It seems to me that at the coming air conference some suggestion should be made for using Camp Borden, where we have an air force training school and the Canadian armoured corps, to train the two forces to cooperate and learn the characteristics of each other's weapons, so that as far as the army is concerned, we shall know what we look like from the air, and the air force will know some of the difficulties, the lack of vision, the peculiarities and the strain upon drivers of armoured vehicles in the army. I have made a similar suggestion before. Both the air and the army authorities have invariably agreed that this would be a good idea, but the air force said, "We have not the pilots to train these men, nor have we the machines." I suggest that this is one of the essentials. We should send both our army and our tank crews overseas with some knowledge-you cannot make it extensive, but at least it can be a basic knowledge-of each other's point of view. In this way you will start off with a cooperation which you must have in any mobile war.
There was an announcement in the press the other day that His Majesty the King was pleased to assent to the formation of a Royal Army Air Corps. I have seen nothing further about it, and I should like to know whether there is any foundation for the statement.

I believe it was a Canadian Press dispatch, and appeared in a Toronto paper.
There has been considerable discussion this afternoon and this evening concerning commissioning of air crew personnel who have graduated. The minister suggested that they should become ensigns. The difficulty, I believe, is that after a certain period, when

War Appropriation-Air Services
they go through and get their wings, the highest fifty per cent are commissioned and the rest are made sergeant pilots. I suggest to the minister that he consider giving all graduates the king's warrant-making them all warrant officers-until they have had so many hours combat flying. I suggest that as an idea which might work, because I realize a difficulty arises. Because one boy gets 86 per cent and another gets 84 per cent, the one becomes an officer and the other a sergeant. I believe that is an unfair system. Perhaps there are/ difficulties about making them all officers where there are large bomber crews containing as many as eight men. But this discrimination seems to me bad and undemocratic in principle.
There are two or three more suggestions I should like to make to the minister. A large number of Royal Air Force personnel proceeded here from England and trained in the United States. They came back, and we met them. All of them had a certain amount to say. A large number were failed, and they believe they had been failed unfairly. This is an administration matter, but I must point out that these stories were general; we talked to many who came back. Was there any reason why so large a number did not qualify as pilots in the United States?
Before a man can join the air force he undergoes an aptitude test. I believe that is general, applying to both the ground crew and the air crew. In my opinion there should be an aptitude test for every recruit before entering any branch of the fighting forces, and it would be interesting if the minister would give us some information or suggestions about how this test has worked for his air crews and his ground crews.
