The air crews-pilots, observers and air gunners-go through the schools and train until they get to their combat planes. I believe the committee would like to know what percentage of their training they get in Canada before they are capable of engaging the enemy in a combat plane. I understand they go to a combat centre in England and then to their fighter aerodrome. How much more training could

we do in Canada? What percentage of the finished article is made in Canada? What is left to be done in England?
If section 3 of the National Resources Mobilization Act is done away with, a great deal of time and effort might be saved by having joint recruiting stations. Frequently a man in the army, particularly at a basic training centre, thinks he is unfairly dealt with because he has not had an opportunity to go into the air force, and the military authorities have quite a lot of trouble in convincing him that the air force is full up as regards ground crew and that he has not the qualifications for air crew. I believe it would be a saving if joint recruiting offices for the three services were set up, wherein each applicant would be tested and sent to the service with which he was going to fight. He could then go on, knowing from the very beginning that he had had his chance of joining whatever service he wanted to join. He would not continue during weeks and perhaps months of training with the psychological handicap of wishing that he was in some other service.
I leave these three or four suggestions with the minister, and I would again particularly stress cooperation between the air and the army. We feel that we are kept in the dark about air matters, and there is a certain amount of resentment in many sections because it is believed that the air force does not cooperate with us. I dare say the fault is partly ours, but I think this is a war of three dimensions and, no matter what weapon we fight with, we have to be conscious of air warfare. I would suggest most earnestly to the minister that during the coming conference, right from the basic beginning, cooperation between the army and the air be taught, and taught in such a way that the army will become air-minded and that those in the air force will have a better understanding of our problems on the ground.

I think the eulogy of the flying schools by the hon. member for Halton (Mr. Cleaver) is likely to lead the committee astray. I was on the war expenditures committee last year when the second report was made, and when the subcommittee, of which the hon. member for Halton was chairman, presented its report to the main committee it was not accepted but was referred back to be amended. I see no reason why the commendation should be so effusive even if the flying schools are doing a fairly good job. Why they should make any profit at all is the amazing thing to me. After all, the civil aviation schools put only a very nominal

War Appropriation-Air Services
amount of money into these institutions. All the capital is provided by the government. To set up a school complete, requires, I understand, some $800,000. The original shareholders in the aviation schools provided $35,000, on which they are allowed a dividend of 5 per cent. Why they should make any profit over the 5 per cent paid on the invested capital is quite beyond me.
Let us look at the fourth report of this subcommittee, concurrence in which has not yet been moved in this house. I find this:
The subcommittee finds that in every instance all of these clubs and companies are devoting their entire effort to the war training work. They are highly efficient and are carrying on their task without any thought of profits to the company or to private individuals.
That appears on page 593 of the minutes of proceedings, and two pages further on I find this:
In regard to profits to be earned by the training companies under the agreement, the amount of profit which would accrue under the agreement was determined as accurately as was possible at the time, but there was no previous experience on which to base an estimate. The subcommittee has carefully checked the profits which are being earned and finds them to be excessive, due to increased flying hours necessitated by increase in pupil intake.
Here is an organization which the committee says is carrying on without any thought of profit, and yet in the next breath it finds that the profits that are being made-mind you, by an organization which is working without thought of profit-are excessive. I wonder what the profits would be if they were operating for profit. Certainly they do wonderfully well when they are interested only in performing a public service. I mention this because I refused to accept the recommendation made by the subcommittee when the report was submitted. The government, as I have pointed out, provides the buildings, the planes, the gas, the oil, the food and everything. All that the schools provide is the management, for which they are allowed so much for salaries.
The report, a copy of which I have here, states that the companies operating the flying training schools are doing so under an agreement the terms of which were negotiated after conferences with the Canadian flying club association. It says:
Under the present contract the crown supplies the site of the school and all necessary buildings and equipment. The training company furnishes all management and operating personnel excepting a small supervisory air force personnel resident at the school to maintain proper discipline of the trainees and to see that the syllabus of training is adhered to.
Let us see what the government supplies. The first item is management:
This item includes salary of manager, secretary-treasurer, office staff and all items of management. This payment is a fixed amount of $1,400 per school, per lunar month.
Then there is operation and maintenance:
This item includes the salaries of all instructors, instructor pilots, engineers, electricians, mechanics, labourers, etc., and also includes cost of all spare parts and material used in connection with the maintenance of the aeroplanes. This item also includes heat, light, insurance, etc. The agreement calls for payment of a monthly target price, which in the first agreement was $16,000.
Then flying hours:
This item covers payments for three separate items. A monthly target price is set up to pay for cost of gas and oil. Any surplus earned as to gas and oil is the property of the crown and there is no profit feature to the company in regard to this item in any way.
Then messing:
The sum of 90 cents per man per day is paid the training company for messing. As no provision is made elsewhere in the contract for costs of the caretaking of quarters and for laundry, the training companies are paying for these services out of the amount allowed for messing, and in most instances the messing is sublet to a firm of reliable caterers.
Here we have the whole cost paid for by the government. And remember that in the first instance all the capital that the flying schools supplied was $35,000, whereas the capital required for a school is some $800,000 or more. Despite that, I find in the fourth report something to which I objected at the time the second report was being prepared, and which was not included in that report:
The subcommittee has already recommended that all profits should be invested in noninterest bearing Dominion of Canada bonds so that all profits earned will be available for war purposes until the end of the war. Most of the companies are already following this practice. The subcommittee has already recommended that the agreement should be amended making this compulsory. If this is done and if all the common stock of the training companies is held in trust for the flying clubs sponsoring the training company with federal charters in the terms recommended in this report then the question of profits is adequately protected.
Let me remind you, Mr. Chairman, that this common stock was given to the owners of the original $35,000 capital, and they did not pay anything for it. So the government of Canada is paying dividends or profits on common stock that did not cost the shareholders anything.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: Oh, no.
That is the principle to which I am objecting in this instance. It is a crime and a shame, and for the life of me I cannot see how the committee could recommend such a procedure.

My remarks this evening will be on a different subject and perhaps of a different nature from those which have been made by previous speakers, but I find it difficult to keep my seat when a matter so important to the country generally as the air force of Canada is under discussion.
I believe the Canadian people have a very deep sense of appreciation of the tremendous sacrifices that are being made by a certain group of our citizens, that is, the men who risk their lives day and night in the air crews of the Royal Canadian Air Force and the Royal Air Force itself. It seems to me that if ever a truth was self-evident it is the fact that when the actual testing time comes to our people, the youth of our country always measures up to the very best traditions of both age and experience. Those of us who have carefully watched the work of the men of our air crews are brought to our feet to pay a well merited tribute to these men who night and day sweep the skies over Germany, over the desert sands of Libya and over the expanse of the oceans from one end of the world to the 
other, who take risks perhaps greater than those taken by any other branch of our armed forces, and I say that without desiring to cast any reflection upon the dangers faced by those in our other armed services. But it does seem to me-and I am sure this must have occurred to many members of this parliament as I know it has occurred to many people throughout the country-that if we are to have some approach to equality of sacrifice in this war, and if some men are to be paid more than others, it should be the members of these air crews who face perils and dangers night and day, whose lives at best are very short, and of whom the Prime Minister of Great Britain said in those memorable words which will echo down the corridors of time, "Never was so much owed by so many to so few."
So it seems to me that, while there may be good reasons why in committees like this questions of pay should not be unduly emphasized, at the same time since there is a difference in the amounts paid to the men serving in the civilian as well as in the military branches of our war effort, we should review once and for all the whole question of pay in order to make proper recognition of the dangerous activities which we ask these men to undertake. I know something of the difficulties with which the minister is faced in connection with many of these matters. There are some things for which I do not give the minister credit, but I do believe he is sympathetic to the men in the air force of which he is the head. So I appeal not only to his mind but to his heart, to see to it that these men of the air force are given some sort of return which will compensate them in some measure at least for the tremendous risks and the great dangers which they must face day and night for you and for me.
I should also like to offer a suggestion to the minister in regard to a matter which has come to my attention on more than one occasion, as I am sure it has come to the attention of the minister and other hon. members. It is in connection with the embarkation leave, which particularly to the members of the air crews is a very significant and important leave. It seems to me we should take into consideration the vast distances in this country, and see to it that each man secures his clear fourteen days leave in every instance. I understand that is not always the case in some branches of the service, and I hope that when the minister scrutinizes his own regulations carefully he will make the necessary adjustments. I ask the minister to consider this matter seriously, because nothing less than the best should be given to these men. I

War Appropriation-Air Services
know the minister will see that that is done, after he has given the matter that attention which I suggest it so richly deserves.
What I am about to say, in closing my remarks, was to a great extent prompted by what was said by the hon. member for York West (Mr. Adamson), when he spoke of the desirability of having the three branches of the service united in some kind of joint enlistment bureau. I have no doubt that from time to time the minister has received complaints to the effect that young men attempting voluntary enlistment in Canada have a difficult time in trying to assess the position in which they find themselves. They have difficulty in locating the type of service into which they wish to enter. I have always felt that as a country we have not done enough to provide information leading to the objectives these young men wish to reach. Even if it is rather late, it seems to me that something might still be done. It is better late than never. I believe we could provide voluntary enlistees in Canada with more information as to the available types of service, and the work which may be open to them when they wish to enter any of the three branches.	.
I am sure the minister has had young men come to him-I have had the same experience -and say, "Well, I do not know where to go. I am depending upon a rumour here, and a story there. I am told it is best to go into this branch of the air force, or that branch of the army." It seems to me that the government should take some steps, before it is too late, to see that these men learn through some authoritative channels the types of services and the openings available in the three branches of our armed forces.
Therefore I would supplement what the hon. member for York West had said, with the further suggestion that we might properly have some kind of information bureau to carry out the suggestions which have been made. While at this time I do not wish to tread upon dangerous ground in connection with our present defence position in Canada, there are one or two questions I should like to ask. Of course the minister will be careful in his answers to any questions I may raise in this connection. However, there has been in the minds of many people in Canada the thought of the imminent possibility-perhaps not imminent, but certainly a possibility -of air attack on the dominion. I remember having brought this matter to the attention of the Minister of Pensions and National Health a year ago. I really went quite a piece with him, because I suggested the setting up of a new ministry of home security. I pointed out at the time that the minister knew I was making no reflection upon him, because, having regard to the fact that he is a bachelor, there was no use in giving him home security to look after.
I made the suggestion seriously, however, because I felt, as did many Canadians, that there was a definite possibility of air attack on the dominion. I believe the situation is more imminent to-day than it was then. There are many citizens-you may call them armchair critics, if you like, and among the number you may place me-who think that the dominion should have the assurance that if we are attacked from the air we have in our air force in Canada sufficient combat planes with the necessary equipment, guns and power to see to it that whatever does come across the seas, either from aircraft earners or otherwise, will be dealt with in the manner in which we as Canadians would want our nation defended.
I would therefore ask the minister to give the house and the country some assurance that every possible precaution is being taken, not only in connection with our coastal antiaircraft defences, which I know are being developed, but also with respect to interceptor planes and other types of combat planes. I know we have plenty of trainers; but, on the other hand, that would not be sufficient, provided we were subjected to air attack. Would the minister consider that question and, if possible, satisfy our people by an assurance that the air force in Canada is reasonably able to take care of any emergency such as I have outlined.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: No minister in any country in the world can give the assurance that there is adequate air protection at any time As to telling my hon. friend as to the combat planes and bombers, or interceptor planes we have on hand he knows very well I cannot tell him that.

Just prior to the evening adjournment I asked the minister a number of questions which, I realize, he has not yet had an opportunity of answering. However, the hon. member for Halton took it upon himself to .answer the questions I had asked. I do not wish to enter into any controversy with that hon. member in regard to what took place in the committee on war expenditures, and for that reason I am not going to answer many of the statements he made this evening.
I do, however, wish to point out that no attack was made on any system. The



War Appropriation-Air Services
stand I take now and the one I took last summer was that in a time of war there was no justification for profiteering on the part of any company or any individual in Canada. If the answer to the questions I have asked reveals that there was in fact no profiteering, then of course the entire answer has been given to the questions I asked. This evening the minister said that in so far as air observer companies were concerned, after payments of all income tax and the like the average profit had been $5,000. That, of itself, signifies little. It shows that after all expenses have been paid and all deductions made, these companies have been receiving a net profit of 10 per cent in connection with the doing of work, the producing of air observers, for our flying forces. Let me say that what the true profit is can be determined only when there is an answer to the question I asked as to how much money was paid by the operating companies to the parent companies. The present set-up in some cases is this: There is the parent company. Then there is the company which receives the contract from the government. I suggest to the minister that the records will show that one or more of these companies with contracts, when arriving at a net profit of $5,000, failed to take into consideration sums of money running up to $12,000 and $14,000 which were paid to parent companies that existed before the war. Therefore the true state of affairs is not revealed by the statement that the net profit is merely $5,000.
This afternoon the minister stated that, either yesterday or the day before, the Canadian Pacific Railway company agreed voluntarily to continue the operation of air observer schools without profit. That attitude on their part deserves the highest commendation. The work they are going to do in connection with the training of air observers is the type of service which was so highly spoken of by the hon. member for Peel (Mr. Graydon), and they are going to do it without profit. The object of the questions I asked this afternoon was to place before the minister and the country the situation which prevails in so far as certain companies operating air observer schools is concerned. They are permitted to make profits on an average of $5,000 after having deducted large sums of money which were paid over to parent companies. I understand that, in addition to that profit, 5 per cent has been guaranteed to each shareholder.
The present position is that these companies which were set up by private individuals received contracts from the government, under

which they first received a management fee of $2,700 a month. On the basis of that management fee and the savings thereon, a large portion of their profits is determined. Then there is a maintenance and operation account on which they receive $17,500 for every period of four weeks. At the expiry of their contract they receive 25 per cent of the surplus savings under this particular head. Finally there is the flying profit. Previously they received $1 and then it was reduced to 35 cents. The hon. member for Halton says that this was done voluntarily, but I do not intend to enter into a discussion of the definition of "voluntarily". However, I would point out that the operating companies agreed to do this only after the matter had been discussed before the committee. I ask the minister to furnish the committee and the house with information to which the members of the committee cannot refer because the evidence was given behind closed doors. Will he furnish answers to the following additional questions? What was the gross profit of each company operating an air observer school?

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: Are these the questions the hon. member sent me this afternoon?

I shall send these over to the minister. First, I want to know the gross profit of each company operating an air observer school in Canada before the deduction of any taxes. I want to know which companies operating air observer schools paid anything to parent companies for experience and the like. How much was paid by each company to its parent company during the first year of operation? The answers to these questions and to those I asked this afternoon will afford an opportunity to this country and the committee to know whether the contention of the hon. member for Halton is correct or whether the contention I am placing before the committee is correct, namely, that some of these companies are taking an unfair advantage of this country's being at war. I am glad to note the patriotic attitude of the Canadian Pacific Railway.
Better watch the C.P.R. too.
I have the assurance of the minister that the C.P.R. is not getting any profit, and I take it that they are not going to expect any profits from the inception of their contract.
They have other things in mind.

The hon. gentleman may cover that. I say again what I pressed this afternoon, namely, that the Canadian National Railways should have an opportunity of having air observer schools and the like so

War Appropriation-Air Services
that, when the war is over, our two transportation systems will be on an equal footing in so far as the development of post-war air transportation is concerned. I am asking the minister to answer these several questions so that the situation with regard to air observer schools will be known to this committee and to the country.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: Rather than indulge in an acrimonious debate with my hon. friend with respect to this matter, I have taken the liberty of asking the officials who are most familiar with it to prepare categorical replies to his questions. I do not know that it would serve any useful purpose for me to controvert the statements made by my hon. friend, although perhaps if they go out to the press to-night it will be found that a great many of them are not in accord with the facts. However, I am not going to discuss them. I am sure I shall be able to answer every one of my hon. friend's questions in such a manner that he himself will have to admit that some of the aspersions which he casts on either the companies or the department, I do not know which, were not founded on fact. I have not my papers before me, but I am quite sure that there are no profits paid to parent companies by the operating companies. If I am not mistaken, most of the air observer companies have no parent company; they are dealing directly with the department.
The minister has said that I made statements which were incorrect.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: I think so.

If he does not know, then I wish to point out to him that there are companies which have parent companies that, have received varying amounts, as high as
813,000	or $14,000, from the companies holding contracts with the government and paid for experience and other services.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: I will check.

I think the minister was most unfair to me when he said that I was casting aspersions that would not be borne out by the facts, when I simply asked questions for the purpose of having the situation determined.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: It is not fair for the hon. member to draw conclusions from his questions until he has had the answers. That is the only objection I have.

I think my hon. friend wants to be fair to both the elementary and the observer schools. He was a member of the war expenditures subcommittee along with myself, but there is one thing in connection with these schools that has not been pointed
out. They had contracts with the government for three years, and the rate per flying hour was based on forty-eight pupils. After the collapse of France things were stepped up and this number was doubled, with the result that with a few more personnel and a few more planes they were getting a larger number of flying hours per lunar month than was expected when the original contracts were let. When we came to investigate their profits, I must say that I was proud of the men in both the elementary and the observer schools because they came here and assured us that it was not profits they were after, and they voluntarily offered to reduce the flying hour profit in the elementary schools from fifty to twenty-five cents, and in the observer schools from SI to thirty-five cents. It was the increase in the number of pupils which they had to handle that was giving them the greater profits which we considered too much. I do not think that has been brought to the attention of the committee before to-night, and I think in all fairness to the schools it should be mentioned.

Mr. Chairman, I want first of all to commend the minister for having built up from scratch an excellent department. I am quite sure that the Canadian people appreciate the great work that is being done by the air force of this country under the minister's direction.
I want to pay tribute to the thousands of young men, mostly from the high schools of this dominion, who have gone into the air service, and particularly do I pay tribute to several hundreds of those boys who have gone from my own classes in my own school. Tonight I should like to pay especial tribute to the memory of one of those boys, Flying Officer McCormick, who was reported killed in a crash a few weeks ago. He had flown his thirty trips over Germany and had been decorated for bravery, and then he had the sad misfortune to be killed while engaged at a training school in England. While paying this tribute to the courage of these young men and to the great work they have done, I repeat that I am confident that the country as a whole is proud in the main of the work of this particular department.
What I want to say to-night is not by way of criticism but rather to ask for information. Would the minister tell us whether there is any collaboration between his department and the Department of Transport in the location of training schools and aerodromes? We have heard of the great part that aviation will play in civil life when the war is over. Canada is spending vast sums of money on the construction of these schools, and it seems to me that

War Appropriation-Air Services
the taxpayers of this country have a right to expect that these schools, as far as military exigencies will permit, shall be so located that when the war is over they can become a part of a great government-owned commercial air service. But I have been informed that many of our government-owned training schools and aerodromes are being built in waste places where, when the war is over, they will probably be left to fall into dilapidation. I think we have a right to expect that there should be cooperation between the two departments in the location of these schools, and it has been suggested to me that, wherever possible, they should be located where they can easily form part of a government-owned commercial air service after the war.
The second point on which I should like information is this: To what extent does the minister's department collaborate with the Department of Munitions and Supply in the letting of contracts? Actually the only criticism I have heard of the service now under discussion pertains to the letting of contracts.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: If I may answer at once, we do not let any contracts at all. The Department of Munitions and Supply are our contractors.
Does the minister's department not give advice in the matter?

My question was that to which the minister has given answer, whether his department was responsible in any way for the letting of contracts.
A few weeks ago I visited one of the factories near Toronto, a comparatively small plant, and I found that it was working at that time on five different contracts. The walls and ceiling of that plant were littered with wings and other parts of planes made for types of machines which had been abandoned. I was told just this week-end that one of the plants near Toronto is now engaged in manufacturing a machine, many of the parts of which have to be brought from England. That appears to be handicapping to some extent the building up of our air arm, and I have heard a great deal of criticism on that point.
The third matter to which I would direct the minister's attention does not rightly belong to his department but is one in which I think he should be interested. We have a plant at Malton, situated fifteen or twenty miles from the city of Toronto. The roads to that plant are probably among the worst in Ontario. The Department of National Defence, the province of Ontario and the municipalities through which these roads run have been engaged ever

since that plant was built in childish quibbling over whose responsibility it is to keep those roads in good repair. On the night of February 8 of this year those roads were snowbound, and on February 9 the plant was closed down entirely on account of the condition of the roads. During a light snow-storm just before the Easter recess, the last snowfall we had in Ontario, the roads to that plant were so impassable that an official of the company stated to me that 5,000 man-hours were lost because of the road conditions- enough time to build one aeroplane. I have a letter from a representative of three thousand employees in that plant, sent just a week ago, relating that as a result of the rains that had fallen the road to that plant was almost impassable. The wear and tear on tires and springs and the extra use of gasoline made necessary because of the nature of that road are something of which either the minister's department or some other dominion authority should take control. It is definitely hampering our war effort.
We heard an excellent appeal from one of our members that the men engaged in the air force should receive the best possible treatment the country can afford. With that I agree. I have heard from a number of the younger married men in the force who are concerned because the government has not granted to their wives and dependents a cost of living bonus. I should like to call that to the attention of the minister and ask him to let us know what consideration has been given to the matter. Unquestionably the dependents' allowance fixed for these men was fixed before the cost of living bonus came into effect. Since that date the cost of living has gone up; it is costing the wives of our airmen as much to live as it does the wives of our civilians, and there is a feeling abroad among the members of the air force that their wives are as much entitled to a cost of living bonus as are the wives of civilian workers.
There is one-final-matter to which I should like to call the minister's attention. This, I believe, comes under his department: I have had correspondence with his department on this matter. It pertains to the wages paid to a group of civilians known as mess-men, employed by the air force. According to information from the minister's department these men are paid 850 a month, plus 81 a day subsistence allowance. From that the sum of $2.50 a month is deducted, I think for superannuation. These men get $78.50 a month. For three months following August, 1941, they received a cost of living bonus. Then it was discovered that their subsistence allowance had been increased at some time

War Appropriation-Air Services
since what is known as the basic period; and, after having this cost of living allowance for three months, it was cut off without notice, in October, 1941, and has not yet been restored. My correspondence from the minister's department states that representation has been made to the treasury board. Apparently the treasury board's interpretation of the conditions under which a cost of living bonus is to be granted precludes the department of air from paying that cost of living bonus. I should like to call the minister's attention to the fact that a great many of these men are returned men. Many of them are unable to serve their country in any other way; they went into this work feeling that here was one humble manner in which they could serve. My correspondence from the minister's department has this remark, which I am quite sure the minister himself will not approve. It calls attention to the fact that these men are receiving more than stenographers, typists and clerks in class grade I under the civil service commission. There should be no comparison between either the type of work these men are doing or the responsibilities that most of these men undertake-

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext:
That is not much of an
argument, I will admit. Whoever wrote that letter is not very logical.

Many of them are
returned men, and I think they are entitled to more consideration than stenographers and typists in the civil service.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: I agree.

May we have the
assurance of the minister that the plea of this group of workers will be given consideration?

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: I shall be very glad to. I hope I did not write that letter; I certainly would not want to write any letters in which I gave as an argument for a low wage to these men that they are getting as good a wage as stenographers and typists. I will not use that argument, anyway.

Relative to the matter of which the minister spoke just now, regarding cooperation between his department and the Department of Munitions and Supply in the letting of contracts, I asked for a return with regard to the construction of an auxiliary airport in my constituency, and in the return, P.C. 9252, in giving a record of the proceedings, it is stated:
That following the receipt of tenders, the Department of National Defence (Air Service) has advised that an additional 20,000 cu. yds. of cut and fill would be required and that
cedar shingles would be used throughout; and negotiations were carried on with Waterman-Waterbury Manufacturing Company Limited;
That this firm has offered to perform the additional cut and fill at a price of 35 cents per cu. yd. less a reduction of $490 for the change in shingles. This firm has also advised that there is an increase of $2,750 over the original tendered price owing to the lateness of the season.
Apparently it was on the advice of the Department of National Defence for Air that the contract price was increased by something over $9,000.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: In all probability, if we required more work to be done we advised the Department of Munitions and Supply to get it done. We increased our specifications, I assume. That is done every day. If I must have 20,000 more cubic yards of fill, I simply tell the contractor to go ahead and do it. I do not know the cost.
It was just in reply to the statement the minister made that he gave all contracts to the Department of Munitions and Supply and did not give any advice in regard to them.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: I said that the Department of Munitions and Supply was our contractor. When we want a job done or when we want to buy something we simply turn it over to them and ask them to do it or to buy it for us, but we must at least specify what we want and the kind of thing we want and provide specifications of the buildings and the runways or whatever it is we require. We do not ask them to specify for us; we specify, and they carry out the contract.
That is the very thing that an hon. member was asking here.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: No, he did not. He asked me if we did the purchasing. We do not do the purchasing. W7e ask the Department of Munitions and Supply to purchase certain supplies for us, and they do so. If we ask them to manufacture aeroplanes for us, they enter into contracts with the aeroplane manufacturers. We do not go near the aeroplane manufacturers.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: You do the requisitioning.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: We requisition; that is all.
Who is responsible for determining what type of aeroplane a certain factory shall make, and when it shall cease to make that type and start on another?

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext:
We are responsible for determining what types of aircraft we require. We requisition a hundred or a thousand aircraft of

War Appropriation-Air Services
a certain type, and my good friend the Minister of Munitions and Supply goes and gets them made wherever he likes, as far as I am concerned.

First, I should like to congratulate the Minister of National Defence for Air upon the statement he made this afternoon about his department. I think he is to be congratulated upon the success of his department, and I sincerely hope that continued success will attend his efforts for the duration. Coming from a county that has four airports I am naturally air-minded, and I cannot say that the people in that county are not like the hon. member for Brantford City (Mr. Macdonald). I have not heard any complaints in the county of Huron about the nuisance of aeroplanes. In fact, we welcome the drone of the engine to put us to sleep. They fly constantly over my house and, since they are in the air they do not interfere with us on the ground. If Brantford wants to get rid of some of its training schools, the schools can easily be moved to Huron and we will accept them with the ones we have.
I want to ask just a few questions. Take a man being drafted to the army. If he prefers to enlist as a pilot, or elsewhere in the air force, can he be transferred?

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: Hitherto a draftee or trainee has had two months after joining the army in which to make up his mind whether or not he wishes to join the air force, provided we require a man of that particular category or that particular type. The request has been made by the army, however, that we no longer exercise that right since it is not likely that we shall be needing very many more men of types other than air crew.

I understand then that after a man has been sixty days in the army he cannot be transferred into the air force. What has been done by the interdepartmental committee set up by the minister to coordinate all medical services in the army, the air force, the navy and the pensions department? Why have there not been regular meetings?

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: Is that in connection with the war expenditures committee's report?
Yes.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext:
I happen to know something about that committee, because at one time, when the present Minister of National Defence (Mr. Ralston) was away, there was some dispute between the air force and the army, and as I was a bit bothered about it I thought that the best thing to do was to dispose of the question in the old-fashioned,

time-honoured way of setting up a committee. This committee turned out to be a good one. One of the members was a representative of the Department of Pensions; another represented the navy, another the army and another the air, and the committee functioned for the purpose not only of coordinating the work but of endeavouring to avoid duplication. I do not know that it was set up as any particularly stable and formal governmental body, but I do know that whenever the occasion requires, this particular committee functions. I do not remember having seen any reports within the last three or four months, but the Minister of Pensions and National Health says he has seen such reports. I do know, however, they, were excellent, and in many instances they saved a great deal of duplication in different departments.
They do keep reports of the different meetings?

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: Any time my department is interested I receive reports.
Why are there separate medical offices and clinics and separate R.C.A.F. personnel, as well as Australian and New Zealand?

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: Australia and New Zealand are separate countries.
But we have Australian pilots in our commonwealth air training plan, and so has New Zealand as well.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext:
They attend the schools of
the commonwealth air training plan in the same way as Canadians.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: The hon. member is asking if they have separate clinics of their own.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: There is only one clinic.
I mean, separate from the army and navy.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext:
Oh; that is another matter. That involves a large question with regard to separate army and air force medical corps. There was a great deal of discussion at the time the air force decided to separate itself from the army in this regard. The experts inform us that there is a specialty in air force medicine. .As far as ordinary medical care of the men is concerned, I suppose they could get along very well, but there is such a thing as air force medical specialty. They study such questions as air pressure, blackouts, the effect of high altitude on pilots and so on, and I am informed by our medical

War Appropriation-Air Services
people it is essential that we have special studies and special courses in medicine. I am speaking purely as a layman in that matter. It took a long time for me to become convinced that there should be a separate air medical corps, but after a considerable time and perhaps a great deal of pressure and a lot of argument I came to that conclusion. At that time I was Minister for Air, I was also acting Minister of National Defence, and it was a long time before I became convinced of the value of a separate air medical corps. Since then the knowledge, as well as the experience, which I have gained, leads me to believe that it was a very wise measure for us to take. I cannot give the medical reasons. The hon. member for Parkdale (Mr. Bruce), who knows more about it than I do, will possibly controvert the reasons which have been advanced by the men in the air force, but they are quite satisfied that the very best thing that could have been done for the air force itself was to have a separate medical corps.
I appreciate that answer. Are the courses for training the same for the Royal Canadian Air Force, in connection with the commonwealth air training plan, as for the Royal Air Force?

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext:
The R.C.A.F. administers
and manages the joint air training plan. All the pilots who now become members of the home war establishment of the R.C.A.F.-I think this is what my hon. friend means- go through the joint air training plan.

Have these men the latest types of machines for their training, at each
camp?

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: We have established certain types as being those required for training, some at the elementary schools, some at the service flying training schools, some at wireless schools and some at bombing and gunnery schools. Possibly someone else has developed better or more advanced types. I do not know, but my officers advise me that the planes we use are as good1 as any in the world for the purposes for which they are used.
The only reason why I asked that question was that I understand they are getting new machines at Sky Harbour, though I have not had any report on the matter lately.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: What is the name of Sky Harbour in my language? Is that No. 12 school at Goderich?

The elementary training
school at Goderich.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: Some time ago we decided to use a new type, what is known as a low-wing monoplane called the Freshman, to replace the Fleets and Moths. This is because we believe it will be more convenient to have a low, single wing than what we had formerly. This is a change of type which was decided upon well over a year ago. It is now coming into production, but that does not mean to say that the Fleets and Moths, in which our men were trained formerly, are in any way unsafe or undesirable from the point of view of training. The new machines are perhaps a more modern type of training plane, but the Moths and Fleets are similar to the machines on which the British have been training for many years. The Freshman is a United States designed plane which will come into production very shortly.
I have only one further question to ask the minister. Why does the R.C.A.F. need a special refrigeration and cold storage plant at manning pool, Toronto?

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext:
I have no idea whether
they have or have not one.

I have been informed
that this cold storage plant is used to store garbage, which garbage is then sent to the piggeries. Is that correct?

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: I shall be only too glad to find out. I am sure the Minister of National War Services would be glad to learn that we took that much care of our garbage, and that we were saving our garbage for salvage all over the country. However, I shall certainly inquire.

War Appropriation-Air Services
half dozen such men have mentioned this to me, mostly friends of mine in the R.F.C. or R.A.F. who rejoined the army or air force in this war and are not permitted to wear any service ribbon. Two of these are disfigured for life on account of air force accidents. Yet the government does not permit them to wear any recognition or ribbon, whereas boys who had a lovely trip and saw England but no war service can do so. although they did not go under any particular danger. ... I feel flying those okl Jennies, with all the crashes, represented as much danger, and yet X cannot wear even one ribbon. I was talking to-night with . . . He is medical officer in the air cadets, and I imagine later on will be asked to wear a uniform for certain inspections, etc. He is lame and broken nose and jaw, etc., due to crash in the camps last war. Yet he cannot wear a service ribbon of any kind. I think he should be privileged to do so, or any other who volunteered for service in 1917. There must be hundreds of such cases in Canada and it does not seem fair or right. Besides, I think it adds to a soldier's or officer's morale and prestige to be able to wear some recognition of the fact that he was in the service of his own free will.
This matter, which affects those who served in the last war, should, I think, be given consideration. I believe the same circumstances will arise at the end of this war. I realize the minister has a great many other duties to perform, but I would ask that he make a note of this point and see whether some recognition cannot be given these men.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext:
So far as my recollection
goes, the right to wear medals or decorations is a matter of royal warrant. I speak subject to correction, but I am under the impression that neither the Department of National Defence, the Department of National Defence for Air nor even the government of Canada has the right to specify the persons who may wear decorations from the last war. What the authority is in connection with this war I am unable to say, but I think I am pretty accurate when I say that this was all laid down by royal warrant or by a decree of the war office at the end of the last war. My colleague the Minister of Pensions and National Health says he thinks that was the case, but I shall be very glad to look into the matter for my hon. friend.

A moment ago the minister referred a question to me, and I should like to answer him. The medical problems connected with air service are highly specialized, and in my judgment warrant having a separate medical service. I think the minister for air is fortunate in having such a capable officer as Air Commodore Ryan as head of that service. He has spent many years in the study of the problems connected with air flights, and is thoroughly competent in every branch of that work. He has gathered around

him an excellent staff of specialists which ensures that everything possible will be done that medical science can devise for the health and welfare of our airmen.
I might add that the late Sir Frederick Banting did a series of experiments in connection with flights, and particularly as to how changes in altitude and pressure affect airmen. He was taking the result of his work to England, when he met with the fatal accident. That work has been carried on by others, and I am informed that as a result a special apparatus is now about to be made, if it has. not in fact already been completed, which will protect men doing the hazardous task of dive bombing. Formerly many of those men became unconscious while engaged in that operation. It is possible now to maintain pressure by the new apparatus in such a way as to prevent this disaster from happening. I have no doubt that it has been called to the minister's attention.
I wish to commend the minister for his discernment in the selection of the men he has gathered about him to do this particular work and in establishing a separate medical service for the air.

The hon. member for Huron North discussed a question which reminded me of something that is happening at Petawawa camp. He spoke about garbage being kept in a refrigerator. I do not know anything about that, but I do know that at one of these camps the disposal of garbage was found most expensive. However, the authorities got busy, and during the past year they discovered a farmer about thirty miles away from the camp who succeeded in relieving the condition. This farmer was engaged in feeding hogs on an extensive scale. His pens passed inspection; and with the addition of new pens, the purchasing of a couple of trucks and the establishment of a boiling system at the camp, the garbage, instead of being handled at great cost, is handled under more favourable conditions. I believe that formerly the camp authorities had to arrange for digging trenches and burning the garbage. Under present conditions, however, it is boiled, and either once or twice a day it is taken to the farm. The man is feeding from 600 to 800 hogs. Instead of the refuse from the camp being wasted, that food is now being turned into bacon.
The farmer assures me that after being fed the garbage his hogs have made better gains than they did before from the feeding of grain, and his bacon receives a better grading. The waste food which was formerly thrown away is now being turned into thousands of pounds of pork. I do not know whether that

War Appropriation-Air Services
is being carried on in other camps across Canada, but certainly it is a plan worthy of consideration. In this particular instance it is working out exceedingly well. It is a great pity that good food should be wasted when it could he turned into bacon for shipment overseas.
Are the Royal Air Force stations manned by Royal Air Force personnel part of the commonwealth air training scheme?

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: No.
Are any officers of the Royal Canadian Air Force posted to any of those Royal Air Force stations?

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: The Royal Canadian Air Force has a kind of general control over the Royal Air Force schools, and it so happens that frequently-I cannot say the number of occasions-officers and men of the Royal Canadian Air Force are posted to Royal Air Force schools, in the same way that Royal Air Force men are frequently posted to us.

Then, as I understand it,
when the United States entered the war there were many United States citizens in the Royal Canadian Air Force. At that time they were given the option of remaining in the Royal Canadian Air Force or of being transferred to some service in their own country. I have in mind a specific case of a man who came from the United States, enlisted in the Royal Canadian Air Force and was given a commission. When the United States entered the war that officer applied to his commanding officer, and offered him his resignation. This was a Royal Air Force station, by the way. The resignation was accepted, but for some reason this man has been kept running back and forth between his home in the southern United States and Ottawa. He has had to run between the Royal Air Force station where he was stationed, and Washington; and for a period of three months-

Did this United States
citizen happen to be a member of the Royal Air Force or the Royal Canadian Air Force?

The Royal Canadian Air
Force. He was kept running back and forth, and as a result was put to great expense for three full months before his discharge from the Royal Canadian Air Force became effective. Meantime he found himself unable to enter any of the services of the United States because-the minister shakes his head, but I have this on the authority of the man himself-the authorities at Washington could not take this man into the United States service until his discharge from the Royal Canadian Air Force became effective.
I bring this to the minister's attention because I believe that when a man comes from another country, offers his service and his life to fight for this country, and is then given the option of transferring back to his native land, it certainly does not reflect any gratitude on our part to place him in a position where he is kept out of all service and, as I understand, without pay, for a period of three months. I draw this matter to the attention of the minister in the hope that it will not recur in the future.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext:
I should be very glad if
the hon. member would in confidence send me the name of the officer, so that I could check up. But the whole question with respect to the return of United States officers and men in the Royal Canadian Air Force has been definitely settled. Negotiations went on for some time. I may add that from the moment the United States entered the war instructions were given in a broad and general way that, provided the United States government held out something for the individual to do, there would be no objection to the United States citizen returning to his own country.
Since then, I believe about two or three months ago, a general agreement was arrived at with the United States government whereby United States citizens serving in the Canadian forces who wished to transfer to the United States forces could signify their desire before a certain date, either the 1st of April or the 1st of May. As a consequence of this agreement a travelling board of officers of the United States forces is going through the country interviewing members of the forces to ascertain just how they will fit into the United States forces. Up to the present time, out of 4,451 United States citizens in the Royal Canadian Air Force, 1,961 have signified their desire to transfer to the United States forces. The cases of these men are being looked into by this travelling board of United States officers, to which I believe some of ours are attached.

The minister has made it quite clear that there will be no new air schools built in the immediate future. However, quite often we see in the papers that the commonwealth air training scheme is to be expanded and new schools opened. This always brings up the question of where they are to be located. Some hon. members have complained about the roads to the schools; others have complained about the noise and about the taxes; but I can assure the minister that if there is any possibility of developing schools in a large portion of southern Alberta, there will be no trouble about roads and taxes and there will be nobody to kick about the noise.

Air Services
There are places there which feel that they have been overlooked in the location of war activities. There are many places with good water facilities, and there are other sections where the government itself has land reserves, like Bassano, Bow Island and Foremost, in Alberta.
The minister stated that some of the present air schools may be enlarged. I hope, when that matter is being considered, he will take into account the success which has been achieved in certain schools. Sometimes we wonder why some schools are located where they are with the wind and snow and rough country and so on. Other schools with more suitable flying conditions have been able to show a greater number of flying hours. Would the minister suggest what the considerations will be in determining what schools will be enlarged?

The minister has said that the general supervision of the R.A.F. establishments in this countiy was given to the R.C.A.F. I have heard boys who were in the R.C.A.F., serving at some stations with the R.A.F., complain that the food is not as good in the R.A.F. station as it is in our own. Apparently the food in our own establishment is excellent in every respect.
While I am on my feet I want to say how pleased I was to hear the minister say this afternoon that he hoped some steps would be taken to eliminate the distinction between sergeant pilots and pilot officers. I do not know if any other member of the party which was in England has mentioned this before, but when we were there we visited a bomber station one evening and met a number of pilot officers who approached us and asked us, when we had an opportunity, to endeavour to persuade the authorities to establish a joint mess. The officers and the sergeants flew together, lived together and sometimes died together, and yet when they got back to the base they were separated. They wanted a place where they could meet together, talk over operations and generally be comradely after the show was over. We took the matter up in London with Mr. Massey and, I believe, also with the British authorities. I am bringing this to the attention of the minister so that if nothing can be done in the other matter, that is with the imperial authorities, at least at our own stations some arrangement may be made whereby the sergeant pilots and the pilot officers can be together.

I should like to ask a question with regard to the difference in pay of men in the R.C.A.F. and men in the R.A.F. Is the difference in the pay of our men attached to the R.A.F. credited to their account, or is it paid to them during their service on the other side?

In view of the announcement made by the Minister of National Defence for Naval Services (Mr. Macdonald) about the sinking of a freighter in the St. Lawrence river, and in view of what has been said about cooperation among the navy and army and air force, would the minister care to say a few words?

Has consideration been given to setting up an air command for the St. Lawrence region?

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: We have an eastern air command which covers the whole of our defensive aerodromes on the east coast, including the St. Lawrence river.
Would it be better to have the St. Lawrence command separate?

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: I hardly think so.

I should like to express my appreciation of the manner in which the minister reviewed the activities of

War Appropriation-Air Services
the air force so comprehensively and without encumbering his statement with too much detail. His statement to-day, following the one he gave last fall, furnishes the basis for a few questions. But first I should like to pay tribute, like so many others have done, to the gallant boys of the Royal Canadian Air Force. Just in passing, I might say that I was at a service on Sunday of the Upper Canada college boys, and old boys, where it was announced that over 650 of the boys and old boys of the college are now in the service of their country.
An eloquent plea has been made by the hon. member for Peel and several other hon. members that th^ dependents of the boys in the air force should get the cost of living bonus. I heartily concur in their suggestion. I feel it is a great pity that there should be that gap following the time a man is reported missing during which no allowance is paid. It is the mothers of the boys who are joining the air force that I have particularly in mind. Remember, these lads in the air force are younger than the men in the army. We have persistently argued that a dependent mother should be treated, in the matter of allowance, in the same way as the wife, and it is a great pity that that so far has not been done. I know of a young lad in the air force whose mother has been supported by his brother and sister. They have their home, but the father is out of the picture. The boy in the air force is giving his mother $20 a month; I presume that is assigned pay. But now the brother who has been helping to support the mother has been called up. He had wanted to enlist but felt himself unable to leave his mother in her present circumstances. I do not know what will happen now, because there is only the sister left at home. It seems to me that we should not approach this question of an allowance from the point of view of giving charity or asking ourselves: What is the least we can get away with? But that is the way we are treating the mothers to-day, and it must be remembered that it is mostly the mothers who are the dependents of the young boys in the air force. I do not think we should consider how small an amount we can give to the mother who has been dependent on her boy who has joined the air force.
The Minister of National Defence asked the other day: "What are we depriving her of?" That seems to be the basis the government goes on. But I would point out that not only the mother I speak of, but many others are going to be deprived of $20 a month, plus the boy's assigned pay of $20 a month, and that is something which certainly should receive further consideration by the minister and the government.
Another matter has been drawn to my attention. A mother had not heard from her son for a long time. She wrote to me, and I took the matter up with the minister's secretary. She did not know where to get hold of her son or how she could communicate with him.
I received a letter from her to-day by special delivery. I am sure that there are many more mothers in her position, because the air force is so widespread in its operations that mothers have difficulty in knowing just where their sons are. This particular mother has not heard from her boy in the air force for seven months. I should be glad if the minister would tell the house and the country how that mother can reach her boy by cable in England or some other place. I have told her where she could write, but after not hearing from him for seven months she wants to send a cable.
Last year I put a question on the order paper with reference to the grounding of planes for overhaul and repair, and the minister gave an interesting reply. I have not the figures here, but he will no doubt remember. It would be interesting to know how much shorter is the period now required for overhaul and repair, with the modern methods and new equipment of to-day at the various schools. Perhaps the minister, without going into too much detail, would pick out a few types of planes and state for how long a period they now have to be grounded for overhaul and repair.
The special committee on war expenditures presented a report on "salvage" and said, referring to the chief salvage officer:
The officer above referred to stressed the point that salvage is not chiefly a matter of disposal of waste goods but in the better sense is a saving of these goods by repair for further use.
The board has only recently come into existence and its work has just commenced, and therefore the committee was not able to pass any final judgment on the work being done hy this board, but is of the opinion that if the programme as outlined is carried out it should result in very substantial economies.
It was indicated to the subcommittee that this board will function solely in the army, that it is somewhat of an experiment, and that should it prove successful, its programme would be extended to include the air force and the navy.
The people of this country, to-day particularly, in view of the shortage of oil, rubber and other products, want to see no waste, and I would ask the minister whether the air force is functioning in cooperation with this salvage board which has been set up.

I have one hope which
I should like to express to the committee and which I trust all members will share. It is suggested by two remarks which have been made during the course of this debate. The first was made by the minister, when in his fine speech he quoted the Right Hon. Malcolm Macdonald, British high commissioner, as paying high praise to the work of the Canadian air force, but, he added, we did not perhaps blow our own trumpets enough. The second remark was made by the hon. member for Davenport (Mr. MacNicol) when he referred to the exploits of Colonel Bishop and others during the last war. He said, quite properly, that they had electrified Europe. I have the feeling that the hon. member for Davenport would have liked1 to put his tongue to the names of some Canadian heroes of this war if they had come quickly to his lips. But the fact is that they did not, and I suggest to the committee that this brings home to us that we are not making enough of the heroes of the air on whom our whole survival depends to-day. This war is unlike any other war in this respect, that to-day our very existence, the existence and continuation of our institutions, depend not so much on great masses of armies working blindly, but on hundreds and thousands of individual feats of heroism such as have never been matched in the history of the world. I suggest to the committee that we have been carrying on a kind of a Maginot line attitude in respect of our acclaim for the men on whom we depend for our survival. Hon. members will remember that we began the war in a very drab way, without bands and without flags; we did not think they were necessary; we thought they were undesirable. We are finding out how wrong that was. But there is still a hangover in some respects, and I suggest that there is such a survival in respect of the attention being paid ,to particular exploits of individual heroism by our fliers. The fact that the hon. member for Davenport did- not bring his tongue to the name of one Canadian pilot who distinguished himself in this way clearly proves what I have said.
We are proud of what our air force have done. We know that they are doing magnificent things. But I believe that we would be still more proud if we knew the individual exploits of individual fliers, if we knew how many planes they had to their credit. Not long ago I had to make a speech in the United States, and I thought it would be interesting
I Mr. Ross (St. Paul's).]
to them if I could pay tribute to some of their great fliers,-O'Hare and others. I knew how many planes they had to their credit; and I made inquiries of the public relations officers of our air force to find the number of planes that Canadian fliers had to their credit, so that I could tell our United States friends and ask "them to share our pride as we shared theirs. But I could not get the number of planes that Canadian fliers have to their credit, because the numbers are not given out, I was told, by the Royal Air Force.
Already we know that we have some magnificent heroes of the air. There is the man who came back only in the last few weeks and who is now in Ottawa, Larry Robillard, whose record as told in the newspaper? is one of the most astonishing of this or any other war. I am informed that not half the story has been told to the newspapers; it cannot yet be told. There are people like Pilot Officer Dougall of Montreal; Pilot Officer Morin of Ottawa; Pilot Officer Blair Russell; Pilot Officer John Fauquier; Wing Commander Timmerman; Sergeant Duffield.

Pat Christie, and dozens of others who are more or less known by reason of casual mention in the press, but whose names do not mean so much to us Canadians as do the names of the men- that appear week by week in the great United States magazine Life. I suggest that is not good for us. We share the pride of the United States in the exploits of her sons. We need to have pride in our own, and in order to have that pride we must have knowledge. 'The knowledge must be related to the individual, and it must be given quickly, while the matter is new. I suggest to the minister that the whole machine for getting news from the fighting front into the minds and into the hearts of the people of Canada, who need the cheer which the tale of heroism will give, can well be improved. The importance of this is shown by the way in which our own hearts respond to the story of heroism whenever we hear it. Most hon. members must have heard President Roosevelt's great speech on April 28. They must have observed how the last third of his speech was not given to a discussion of great events, great battles; it was not given to a discussion of high policy. He told three simple stories of heroism. He told of Doctor Wassell; he told of the crew of the Squalus, and he told of Captain Hewitt T. Wheless. He closed his three stories by saying of the last named, Captain Wheless, "I hope he is listening"; and twenty or thirty or forty

War Appropriation-Air Services
million people listening in to President Roosevelt hoped that. Our hearts were cheered by those stories of heroism. We know that our own Canadian air force is the equal of any air force in the world. We have a right to be told about it, told about it freely, promptly and in a way which gives full credit to their exploits. It may be said of them as it was said of another fighting force by A. E. Housman:
Their shoulders held the skies suspended,
They stood, and earth's foundations stay.

May I thank my hon. friend for drawing my attention to that. I have often thought that we do not give the credit which we should give to these young heroes of the air force.
One reason is because of the British passion for anonymity. When I was over in England last year I did my very best to induce them to permit our press to get the latest possible news on the deeds of our men. I think the situation has improved to a considerable extent. It was with something of the same idea in mind as my hon. friend who has just spoken had, that I had a list compiled of the commanding officers of the Canadian squadrons overseas. speechtext: Unfortunately we receive our bulletins a little too late so that they are no longer news. They are not what is called "hot news." I should like to give a sample of these bulletins to indicate the work done by some Canadian squadrons overseas. I happened to be reading one last night, and I said to myself that if the opportunity presented itself I might give some of the highlights to the house. speechtext: When I visited the old country last November I gathered that the R.A.F. does not wish to publicize the deeds of individual aviators or individual members of the air crew because, if they do, it will tend to weaken the esprit de corps in the rest of the personnel of the force. Does the minister agree with the official R.AE. point of view, or does he agree with the point of view that I would put forward, namely, that the publicizing of individual exploits would do a great deal to build up the morale not only of the R.A.F. or the R.C.A.F., but of the people generally. Will the minister fight for a change-over generally as far as R.C.A.F. pilots and aircrew are concerned?

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: I definitely and most emphatically disagree with the air ministry, perhaps by reason of our education and our proximity to the United States. The fact is that we are a people who read headlines, though perhaps we do not read enough of what appears under the headlines. At any rate, we make our heroes readily. We can learn to love or hate a person when we are not particularly interested in institutions. The RA.F. as R.A.F. or the R.C.A.F. as R.C-A.F. does not mean much to us, but O'Hara, or O'Shea, or Corbett-
Or Mackenzie.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext:
Yes, or any name like that, means a lot to us, and, as I say, perhaps because of our Hollywood upbringing, we are prone to read headlines. It may not be our fault; it may not be logical. However, we must take the people of Canada as we find them; and I sincerely believe that, to the utmost of our ability, we should make heroes of those of our boys who are heroes, for the sake of the morale of the air force and particularly for the sake of the morale of the Canadian people, who probably need it more than the air force does.
